topics.title: FP8 loss-curve validation: bf16 (main) vs FP8 (PR #7079) at row-13 scale on 64x H100
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

comments.body:
🤖 Full A/B launched 2026-07-17 13:32 UTC after nine smoke rounds: `/mwittmann/fp8val-bf16-full1` vs `/mwittmann/fp8val-fp8-full1` on cw-us-east-02a.

**Final configuration** (revised from the issue body's design during smoke debugging — full trail in `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md`):

- 1 node × 8 H100 per arm (16 total), EP8, **batch 16** × seq 4096, **24000 steps ≈ 1.57B tokens/arm** (≥ the 1.44B that resolved 0.01-level deltas in #6486). Model/optimizer/data/seed as designed (row-13 shapes, MuonH full schedule to zero LR, SlimPajama-6B cluster-local cache, seed 0 both arms).
- Tracker: json_logger (per-step `train/loss` in job logs) — no WANDB key was reachable on the submit host; trajectories will be harvested and plotted here.
- No periodic checkpoints (`FP8VAL_CHECKPOINTS=local`).

**Operational findings from the smoke ladder** (each cost a round; logged for reuse):
1. Multi-host XLA sharded-autotuning rendezvous hangs the 4-node compile → `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false`.
2. `experiments/grug/dispatch.py` forwarded only `XLA_FLAGS`, silently dropping `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` → train tasks ran at the 0.75 default pool and OOM'd; forwarding widened to `XLA_*` (+ `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`) on both experiment branches — candidate for upstreaming.
3. Row-13 (26 unrolled layers) does not fit 4-node FSDP (`data=4`) or 2-node EP16 at B64 on 80GB H100s (program peak 89 GiB; matches the June spike's "B64+L26 HBM wall").
4. **FP8 needs ~4 GB more than bf16 at B32** where the pre-merge bench harness fit — possible memory regression from the main merge or a real-trainer×FP8 interaction; open follow-up.
5. **The 10-minute async time-checkpoint deadlocks the run against training collectives** (all bf16 "NCCL clique stalls" and one FP8 step-10 OOM sit exactly at the first save; reproduced on three different nodes). Avoided here by disabling periodic saves; deserves its own issue.
6. bf16 also stalls NCCL comm-init at mem fraction 0.95 but not 0.90; FP8 needs 0.95. Arms run their proven fraction (allocator pool size does not affect numerics).

ETA: fp8 ~6h, bf16 ~6.7h + ~15 min compile. Results (matched-step deltas, final-loss gap vs the ≤0.01 acceptance bar, cooldown-tail zoom) to follow at completion.

🤖 **Root cause of every training wedge found — and it is neither log reads nor checkpoint saves.**

Full-history post-mortems of all terminal runs (smoke9, full1–full3b) show one identical signature in all five wedges: a **BFC allocator failure to allocate the train step's contiguous scratch chunk** — `bfc_allocator.cc ran out of memory trying to allocate 22.66GiB` (bf16 arms) / `40.68GiB` (fp8 arms) on 1–5 of 8 GPUs — followed ~10 s later by the permanent `Acquire clique` rendezvous stall. Allocator dumps show the pool only ~40% occupied at failure: **fragmentation, not exhaustion**. The device threads whose allocation fails never join the 8-way clique rendezvous, so the remaining ranks wait forever — a silent XLA deadlock instead of a raised OOM.

Both earlier theories are retracted with evidence:
- **Log reads (FP8VAL-003b): refuted.** `iris job logs` is served by the standalone finelog server over on-disk parquet (fed by the logship sidecar); it never enters the task process (the in-task uvicorn is the metrics telltale). Timeline agrees: bf16-full2 *survived* the heavy 400k/600k-line harvests at 18:08 UTC and wedged at 19:09 with no heavy read within 10 min; the blamed 900k harvest ran at 19:19 — after the stall.
- **Checkpoint saves (FP8VAL-003c): demoted to a perturbation.** Single-node saves have no barrier/collective; their alloc/free churn just re-carves the pool (both save-adjacent wedges landed 3–11 s after the commit callback). Checkpoint-less arms died identically after hours of slow fragmentation.

Side finding, now quantified: **fp8's largest step temp is 40.68 GiB vs bf16's 22.66 GiB at the identical B16 config** — the fp8 memory regression to bisect, and why fp8 arms always wedged first (needs 57% of the ~72 GiB pool contiguous).

Mitigation for any resubmit: `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc_async` (VMM-backed, immune to BFC fragmentation — the allocator's own hint). full4 (running) predates this finding and has no such flag; recovery commands are pre-staged with it. Details in logbook entry FP8VAL-004.

🤖 **fp8 memory regression attributed** (compile-only probe, one 8×H100 node, AOT-compiles the exact row-13 step bf16 vs fp8 without running it).

`compiled.memory_analysis()`:

| arm | temp arena | args/output/alias |
|---|---|---|
| bf16 | 22.65 GiB | 29.88 GiB |
| fp8 | 37.67 GiB | 29.89 GiB |

Persistent state (args/output/alias) is **byte-identical** — fp8 adds nothing to params/grads/opt-state. The whole **+15.0 GiB is transient peak** in the single fused train step.

Per-dtype arena composition (from XLA `buffer-assignment.txt`; Δ = fp8 − bf16):

| dtype | Δ (GiB) | what |
|---|---|---|
| f8e4m3fn | **+5.0** | forward fp8 operands |
| u8 (fp8-as-u8) | **+3.3** | transposed dual-write fp8 operand copies |
| f8e5m2 | **+0.8** | backward fp8 gradient operands |
| f32 | +4.1 | scale / dequant / amax / accumulation scratch |
| bf16 | +4.0 | extra intermediates around quantize ops |

**The bf16 arena contains zero float8 tensors; the fp8 arena adds ~9 GiB of float8-family data.** XLA materializes each large linear's quantized operand *and its transposed layout for the backward GEMM* and keeps them resident across the fused forward+backward, rather than requantizing in each GEMM prologue. The +4 f32 and +4 bf16 are the requantization scaffolding. So this is dual-write/mixed-dtype operand residency — **not** custom_vjp remat-pinning (bf16 grew only ~4 of the 15 GiB).

Highest-leverage reduction: recompute the transposed fp8 operand in the backward instead of stashing it (the e4m3 + u8-transpose pair is ~8.3 GiB). Real fp8-wiring overhead, tracked as a follow-up separate from the loss validation. Probe: `experiments/grug/moe/fp8val_mem_probe.py`; logbook FP8VAL-005.

Separately, the training wedge (FP8VAL-004) is fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement — note this is the JAX var, not TF's `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`). bf16 control now clears the fragmentation cliff; both arms running.

🤖 **RESULT: loss-curve gate PASSED.** Both arms completed the full 24,000-step schedule (1.57B tokens/arm) cleanly on the `cuda_async` allocator — `fp8val-fp8-full4` and `fp8val-bf16-full6`, seed 0, identical data order.

**Matched-step train loss (FP8 − bf16), all 23,998 steps:**
- mean **+0.0039**, median +0.0038, σ 0.0028, max single-step |Δ| 0.14 (noise)
- no growth: first 2k +0.0034 → mid +0.0029 → **cooldown tail (last 10%) +0.0040**
- final 200-step mean loss: **bf16 3.084 / FP8 3.088 → +0.0040**

**Verdict: PASS** — final matched-step gap **+0.0040**, well inside the ≤0.01 bar (#6486), flat through the cooldown tail (the region #6486 flagged as where precision gaps surface), no NaNs/Infs. Enabling FP8 (wire+dense+grouped GEMMs) does not perturb the training loss at row-13 scale.

**Throughput:** 70.1k / 73.9k tok/s (**1.055×**), MFU 15.09% / 15.92%. On wall-clock (x rescaled by ∫1/throughput), FP8 reaches any given loss ~4.4% sooner and finished 24k in **6.03h vs 6.31h** (~17 min ahead).

Final artifact (4 panels — loss vs step, loss vs wall-clock, Δ with ±0.01 band, throughput): https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32

**Two infra findings from the campaign (both tracked, neither blocks the gate):**
1. Every training "wedge" was a **BFC fragmentation OOM → silent NCCL clique deadlock** at ~42% pool occupancy — *not* heavy log reads or checkpoint saves (both investigated and exonerated). Fix: `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement). Worth landing as the default for FP8 grug runs.
2. FP8's transient step arena is **1.66× bf16** (+15 GiB), attributed by a compile-only probe to the **cast-transpose dual-write** (caching the transposed FP8 operand for the backward) — a deliberate TE-style speed optimization, bounded and sharding-friendly, not a blocker. Follow-up for #7079 if a memory-marginal config adopts FP8.

Logbook `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` (FP8VAL-006) sealed with full TL;DR.

🤖 **W&B:** the two validation trajectories are now in `marin-community/marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079` (full 24k-step per-step `train/loss` + throughput + MFU, history CSVs attached as artifacts):

- bf16 control: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8val-bf16-control
- FP8 (PR #7079): https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8val-fp8
- group (both overlaid): https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079

Backfilled post-hoc from the harvested json_logger histories (the runs used `json_logger` at train time — no `WANDB_API_KEY` on the launch box). Reproducible via `experiments/grug/moe/fp8val_wandb_backfill.py` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`. Final losses match the reported values (bf16 2.909 / FP8 2.911 at step 23,999).
@dlwh Added a managed experiment TL;DR block summarizing the FP8 loss-curve pass, key W&B/artifact links, and the two non-blocking infra findings.

topics.title: [tpu-inference] Qwen3.5 hybrid GDN prefill ~10x slower than pure attention on v6e
topics.body:
Serving Qwen3.5-9B (hybrid GDN attention, `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) on v6e-8 at fork main (`e8809d49`), prefill runs at ~6-7k prompt tokens/s through the `chunked_jax_pd` kernel — roughly 10x slower than Qwen3-8B's pure-attention prefill on the same slice. The engine sits at ~2 running requests with KV cache 0.1% used, so the batch is kernel-compute-bound, not budget- or memory-bound; raising `max_num_batched_tokens` 512 -> 2048 changed neither throughput nor concurrency.

Observed impact: a full 5-shot MMLU (56k echo+prompt-logprobs requests) takes ~3.2h for Qwen3.5-9B vs ~3-10 minutes for Qwen3-8B on identical hardware and pins. Decode throughput looks unremarkable; the gap is prefill.

Repro: serve `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` on v6e-8 (defaults, tensor_parallel per the sizing heuristic), then drive prompt-heavy traffic, e.g. lm-eval `local-completions` MMLU with `echo=True` + prompt logprobs at concurrency 16. Watch prefill tokens/s in the engine stats.

Marin-side context: marin-community/marin#7345 (eval system) — the Qwen3.5-9B column of the eval grid pays this cost on every MMLU-class run.

comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

Actionable — clear repro, named kernel, expected vs actual, and good reporter diagnosis (compute-bound: ~2 running reqs, KV 0.1%, insensitive to `max_num_batched_tokens`).

But the slow code is **not in this repo**. The `chunked_jax_pd` TPU Pallas GDN-prefill kernel and `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` live in the `marin-community/tpu-inference` fork; Marin only pins its SHA. No Marin-side config change fixes a 10x kernel-compute gap, so this is a fork-side kernel investigation rather than a Marin PR.

**Relevant code (Marin side — knobs, none of which are the fix)**
- [`pyproject.toml#L182-L183`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/pyproject.toml#L182-L183) — pins fork `rev 734d2842` (reporter served fork main `e8809d4` — tip skew).
- [`serving_backend.py#L150-L152`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/serving_backend.py#L150-L152) — `max_num_batched_tokens=512`; reporter's 512→2048 no-op is consistent with compute-bound.
- [`vllm_server.py#L119-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L119-L123) / [`serve_and_eval.py#L116-L119`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/evalchemy/serve_and_eval.py#L116-L119) — `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` is **GPU-only** (FlashInfer-vs-triton); the TPU path goes through `chunked_jax_pd` and this flag does not touch it.
- [`quick_serve.py#L114-L154`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/quick_serve.py#L114-L154) — TP-size heuristic; not the bottleneck (batch is compute-bound, not sharded-comm-bound).

## Proposed approach (fork-side, human review before implementation)

Root cause is in the fork's TPU GDN chunked prefill kernel. The signature — 10x vs pure attention, compute-bound, flat under batch-size changes — points at the gated delta-rule chunk recurrence in `chunked_jax_pd` being poorly tiled on v6e: likely a small chunk length serializing the intra/inter-chunk scan, or the GDN state-update matmuls not saturating the MXU (vs. Qwen3-8B attention which does).

Next steps:
1. TPU-profile `chunked_jax_pd` on a Qwen3.5-9B prefill in `marin-community/tpu-inference` (fork main); capture chunk length, MXU utilization, and scan structure.
2. Fix (chunk-tiling / MXU packing / chunk-parallel form) lands in the **fork**, then a Marin pin bump via `.agents/skills/refresh-tpu-vllm-forks/`.

Not opening a Marin PR — the fix is out-of-repo and kernel-scoped. Suggest routing to the tpu-inference kernel owner and tracking against #7345.

topics.title: [datakit] Replace shuffle-store bucket_token_hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass
topics.body:
## Description
`build_clustered_store_shuffle` (`experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store_shuffle.py`) sizes each `(cluster, quality)` bucket's subshard count from a prior store's per-bucket token mass, loaded via `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact`. This couples the builder to a prior artifact and has a chicken-and-egg on the first build: with no prior store it falls back to `default_subshards`, and no constant wins both goals — `1` sends the hot ~651B-token bucket through one multi-hour / OOM-prone reducer, while a flat `K` re-splits small buckets into many tiny caches (the object proliferation #6687 is fixing).

Replace the prior-artifact hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass: a first map pass that runs the join and counts docs (or tokens) per `(cluster, quality)` — small columns, no payload shuffle — then sizes subshards from the measured distribution. Removes the prior-artifact dependency, is correct on the first run, and adapts to distribution drift, at the cost of one extra cheap pass.

Follow-up to #6687 / PR #6725. Parent: #6037.

### Definition of Done
- `bucket_token_hint` param and `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact` removed from `datakit_store_shuffle.py`
- subshard sizing derived from an in-run per-bucket count pass (reads decon/cluster/quality small columns; no tokenize payload, no scatter)
- hot buckets fan out while small buckets stay at one cache, with no prior artifact required
- `test_datakit_store_shuffle.py` covers pre-pass sizing (a skewed synthetic bucket splits without a hint)

topics.title: [grug] Pick a single config.json naming contract for the Snowball HF export
topics.body:
> **Decision requested:** approve Option A (or make the case for B). This gates the export re-cut for publishing Snowball to Hugging Face (#7366). Origin of the ask: [@ClassicLarry in #6811](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4970625865): *"Recommend we clean up the config to standardize against hugging face before we do that."* cc @ClassicLarry ## Problem `config.json` is the first file anyone — human or library — reads to learn a model's shape. Ours currently says most things **twice**. The exporter (`to_hf_config`, `experiments/grug/moe/model.py:228-265`; mirrored in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py`) writes 11 fields under both their grug name and their Hugging-Face-style name: ```jsonc "hidden_dim": 2560, "hidden_size": 2560, "num_experts": 256, "num_local_experts": 256, "num_layers": 26, "num_hidden_layers": 26, "intermediate_dim": 1280, "intermediate_size": 1280, "moe_intermediate_size": 1280, // … 11 duplicated fields in total ``` This was a deliberate hedge: our three loaders (marin vLLM fork on GPU, tpu-inference on TPU, Levanter re-import) each prefer different names, and writing both meant none had to change. It works — but it's the wrong thing to freeze into a public artifact: 1. **The two names can disagree, and no one arbitrates.** The loaders don't pick the same winner: the vLLM fork mostly prefers the HF name, Levanter and tpu-inference prefer the grug name. If a pair ever disagrees (hand edit, future exporter bug), GPU and Levanter silently load *different models from the same file*. Only TPU serving would notice, as a side effect of an unrelated integrity check. 2. **Published keys are forever.** Once on HF, external code gets written against whatever keys we ship. Keys can be *added* later without breaking anyone; they can never be removed. Shipping the redundant set freezes it, on a model that is still evolving. 3. **It looks unfinished** — which is exactly what the "standardize against HF" ask is about. **Why fixing this is cheap:** every loader tries the grug name, then the HF name, then a default — and none complains about extra or missing keys. So any config that carries *one* name per field loads on all three backends today, with **zero loader changes** (audit: Appendix 1). ## Options ### Option A — standard `transformers` names for core fields + the most common public spelling for MoE fields (recommended) Core fields (hidden size, layer/head counts, …) have one universal spelling across the entire `transformers` ecosystem — use it. MoE fields have no universal spelling, so use the most common one per field (survey of 10 public MoE families: Appendix 2). The result happens to equal Qwen2-MoE's key set — convenient, since Qwen2-MoE is also grug's closest structural relative (shared expert + sliding window + GQA): ```jsonc { "architectures": ["GrugMoeForCausalLM"], "model_type": "grug_moe", "dtype": "bfloat16", // core — universal transformers names "vocab_size": 128256, "hidden_size": 2560, "num_hidden_layers": 26, "num_attention_heads": 20, "num_key_value_heads": 5, "head_dim": 128, "max_position_embeddings": 65536, "sliding_window": 2048, "rms_norm_eps": 1e-5, "initializer_range": 0.0098821, "rope_theta": 10000.0, "tie_word_embeddings": false, // MoE — most common public spelling per field (== Qwen2-MoE's set) "num_experts": 256, "num_experts_per_tok": 4, "moe_intermediate_size": 1280, "shared_expert_intermediate_size": 2560, // grug-specific (no public equivalent) "qk_mult": 1.5703274004183787, "grugmoe_attention_mode": "production", "grugmoe_artifact_schema_version": 1 } ``` Bare `intermediate_size` is deliberately absent: in most MoE configs it means the *dense* MLP width, which grug (all layers MoE) doesn't have — publishing it as the expert width would mislead exactly the tools we're trying to be legible to. ### Option B — grug's own spelling for every field Keep the `GrugModelConfig` names for the 11 duplicated fields: `hidden_dim`, `intermediate_dim`, `shared_expert_intermediate_dim`, `num_experts`, `num_experts_per_token`, `num_layers`, `num_heads`, `num_kv_heads`, `max_seq_len`, `layer_norm_eps`, `initializer_std`. Everything else as in A. ### Option C — keep writing both names (status quo), optionally + an equality check Today's output is unambiguous only because the exporter writes equal values to every pair. Adding an equality check (exporter and all three loaders) would close the divergence risk — at the cost of freezing the full redundant surface publicly *and* adding validation code in three repos. Strictly more surface and more code than either single-name option. ## Comparison | Criterion | A | B | C (+check) | |---|---|---|---| | Loads on all 3 backends today, unmodified | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | A disagreeing name-pair is impossible | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (✅ only with new validators in 3 repos) | | Core fields use the universal `transformers` names | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | | Keys match training code / `.executor_info` | MoE partly | ✅ | partly | | Smallest frozen public surface | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ## Recommendation: A For core fields, "standardize against HF" has an unambiguous meaning — one spelling shared by every family we surveyed — and A adopts it. For MoE fields no standard exists, so A takes the most common spelling per field; the truly grug-specific keys (`qk_mult`, …) then stand out instead of drowning in duplicates. External readers see a config that looks like the ecosystem they already know. On upstreaming (#7367 — deliberately deferred until the arch stabilizes): no upstream schema exists yet, and `transformers` has standard machinery for accepting alternate names (`attribute_map`), so B would not *force* a rewrite. But whatever we publish becomes a compatibility requirement on the eventual upstream class, and upstream convention makes the standard names the likely primary spelling — so under B that class carries grug aliases indefinitely, or the published config re-grows the HF names later. Some form of the duplication this issue removes comes back; A minimizes it. **The case for B** (recorded, because it nearly wins): config keys = training dataclass fields = `.executor_info` — one grep surface, no mental mapping; and since no stock library can load `model_type: "grug_moe"` anyway (even the Hub's parameter badge reads the weights files, not config.json), standard names buy less than they appear to. If we weight internal coherence over external legibility, B is defensible — that call is what this issue is for. ## Mechanics / DoD (this issue) - `to_hf_config` (both copies) writes single names per the chosen option; `from_hf_config` **keeps** its fallbacks so existing dual-name artifacts still load. - **Contract test at export time:** assert the final `config.json` (after `config_overrides` merge, which could sneak an alias back in) has exactly one key per duplicated field, no banned aliases, and the right values; then load it back through Levanter's `from_hf_config` and compare field-by-field. This matters because every loader silently substitutes defaults for missing keys — e.g. Levanter's `vocab_size` default happens to equal Snowball's real 128256, so a dropped key would look "correct" by pure luck. - GPU/TPU coverage needs nothing new: the backend-parity suite (#7314) re-run on the re-cut export already loads the real config paths end-to-end. - `grugmoe_artifact_schema_version` **stays `1`** — tpu-inference hard-requires `== 1`, and all shipped loaders handle the reduced key set. - Scope: this contract governs the *published* config.json only; what a loader re-serializes from memory is out of scope. - Handoff: the publish task (#7366) re-cuts the bf16 export — weights unchanged, so the logprob parity goldens don't change — which regenerates `SNOWBALL.export_sha256` and the hash-named `export_uri`, re-runs parity, and uploads that exact tree. ## Open sub-decision - Prefix the grug extras (`qk_mult` → `grugmoe_qk_mult`)? The pinned fork reads bare `qk_mult`; proposal: bare for v1, revisit at upstreaming. ## Related issues - #6811 — Snowball hero run; the publish discussion and the config-cleanup ask live here. - #7366 — publish Snowball to HF; this decision is its config prerequisite. - #7367 — upstream Grug to vLLM/transformers; deferred, but the naming chosen here seeds it. - #7097 — consolidate the vLLM forks; where loader-code unification belongs (not here). - #7314 — backend-parity tests on representative prompts; the re-verification harness for the re-cut export. ---
Appendix 1 — loader audit (who reads which names) References at the pinned serving revisions (vllm fork `afb26719…`, current tpu-inference / marin main). Tuples = the order each loader tries names. | Field | vLLM fork | tpu-inference | Levanter re-import | |---|---|---|---| | hidden | `(hidden_size, hidden_dim)` — HF-first | `(hidden_dim, hidden_size)` | `(hidden_dim, hidden_size)` | | expert FFN | `(intermediate_size, moe_intermediate_size, intermediate_dim)` | `(intermediate_dim, moe_intermediate_size, intermediate_size)` | same as TPU | | shared-expert FFN | `(…_size, …_dim)` | `(…_dim, …_size)` | `(…_dim, …_size)` | | experts | `(num_experts, num_local_experts)` — grug-first even here | same | same | | experts/token | `(num_experts_per_tok, num_experts_per_token)` | `(num_experts_per_token, num_experts_per_tok)` | same as TPU | | layers / heads / kv-heads / seq len / eps / init | HF-first | grug-first | grug-first | | `vocab_size` | default 32000 → caught later by weight-shape checks | **required** (parse error if absent) | default 128256 (= Snowball's real value — silently "correct") | | `sliding_window`, `qk_mult`, `rope_theta` | single-name, silently defaulted | same | same | | `model_type` | registry key | **required** `== "grug_moe"` | **required** | | `grugmoe_artifact_schema_version` | not read | **required `== 1`** | optional | Key properties: every duplicated field is accepted under either spelling by all three loaders; none rejects unknown keys; the fork's config class re-creates both spellings internally after parsing, whichever was present. tpu-inference additionally re-reads the raw JSON as an artifact-integrity gate (schema version + field-by-field cross-check against the serving config + exact tensor-name set) — which is why a *disagreeing* name-pair raises on TPU, and why required/default behavior differs per loader (hence the explicit contract test rather than reliance on defaults).
Appendix 2 — survey: MoE key spellings across 10 public model families Fetched from each repo's raw `config.json` (Mixtral from knowledge; repo gated): Mixtral, Qwen2-57B-A14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V3, OLMoE, gpt-oss-20b, Phi-3.5-MoE, GLM-4.5-Air, Hunyuan-A13B, Kimi-K2. | Field | Spellings found (count) | Winner | |---|---|---| | top-k | `num_experts_per_tok` **(9/10)**; `moe_topk` (Hunyuan) | `num_experts_per_tok` — de-facto standard | | expert count | `num_experts` (Qwen2, Qwen3, OLMoE, Hunyuan — **4**); `num_local_experts` (Mixtral, gpt-oss, Phi-3.5 — 3); `n_routed_experts` (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi — 3) | `num_experts` — plurality, and grug's own name | | expert FFN width | `moe_intermediate_size` (Qwen2, Qwen3, DeepSeek, GLM, Hunyuan, Kimi — **6**); `intermediate_size` doubling as expert width (Mixtral, OLMoE, gpt-oss, Phi-3.5 — 4) | `moe_intermediate_size` — majority, and unambiguous | | shared-expert width | `shared_expert_intermediate_size` (Qwen2 — the **only** family expressing shared experts as a width; DeepSeek/GLM/Kimi/Hunyuan use a *count*, `n_shared_experts`/`num_shared_expert`) | `shared_expert_intermediate_size` — only exact-fit precedent | So Option A's MoE set is not "Qwen is the standard" — it's the per-field most-common (or only-fit) spelling, whose union equals Qwen2-MoE's set. Core fields (`hidden_size`, `num_hidden_layers`, `num_attention_heads`, `num_key_value_heads`, `rms_norm_eps`, `max_position_embeddings`, `vocab_size`, `rope_theta`, `tie_word_embeddings`) are spelled identically in **all** surveyed families.

topics.title: [TPU] Add June 67B inference parity
topics.body:
Add the two TPU cells missing from the June 67B inference parity suite. This does not add or test the experimental Snowball inference backend.

- Revalidate the vendored June Levanter model on one `v6e-8` against a same-schema TPU golden.
- Compare the same BF16 export through TPU vLLM at TP8 across all 64 prompts through 32K.
- Restore checkpoint arrays in the exemplar dtype so the BF16 native oracle fits on `v6e-8` without first materializing FP32 device weights.

The existing GPU cells, shared comparator, persisted report, and prompt fixture remain the common path. The TPU-vLLM ceilings for 256, 1K, 4K, 16K, and 32K are `0.04`, `0.125`, `0.10`, `0.70`, and `0.50`.

This PR is stacked on [#8431](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8431), which pins the immutable vLLM/tpu-inference wheel pair qualified and promoted after [vLLM #47](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/47).

> [!NOTE]
> Current head `1f575cd3b5` is ready for code review. Its accelerator cells are intentionally deferred until after that review.

<details>
<summary>Current-head checks</summary>

- 33 TensorStore restore tests pass.
- 11 shared parity and cluster-definition tests pass.
- 68 external-dependency and serving tests pass.
- All six accelerator cells collect without running them.
- Lock, generated dependency descriptors, changed-file lint, and automated review pass.
- GitHub CI is green at the exact PR head: 32 checks observed, with no failures or pending jobs.
- The broad diff-driven run reported 948 passes and 7 skips. Its three parallel-load failures all passed serially with the same 60-second timeout and unchanged source.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Prior numerical qualification</summary>

The three TPU-vLLM captures behind the retained parity commits were byte-identical. Their bucket maxima were `0.034459`, `0.118812`, `0.096751`, `0.594441`, and `0.375904`; every greedy token matched.

| Cell | Prior Iris job | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Native June Levanter GPU | `/romain/snowball-checkpoint-inference-99bf5b02` | Exact GPU-golden match |
| Exported Levanter GPU | `/romain/snowball-parity-levanter-72d2623d` | Pass; max error `0.068273` |
| vLLM GPU PP1 | `/romain/snowball-parity-vllm-pp1-cf28c4f6` | Pass; max error `0.073122` |
| vLLM GPU PP2 | `/romain/snowball-parity-vllm-pp2-0d89b782` | Pass; max error `0.077773` |
| Native June Levanter TPU | `/romain/snowball-tpu-checkpoint-a17fad89` | Exact TPU-golden match |
| vLLM TPU TP8 | `/romain/snowball-parity-vllm-tpu-00550004` | Pass; all bucket ceilings |

These jobs predate the current semantic rebase and do not qualify `1f575cd3b5`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why the first commit changed during rebase</summary>

Current Marin reads checkpoint shards directly with a shared TensorStore context and a process-wide host-memory budget. The exemplar-dtype restore was ported into that reader instead of restoring the removed JAX checkpoint-manager path. It preserves the shared context, byte budget, target memory kind, and save-side memory trimming, while charging the temporary cast buffer to the host budget.

The other three parity commits are patch-identical to the previous PR head.

</details>

Part of #8323.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

comments.body:
🤖 Taken five of six findings in f4299966b.

**Bind loaded model bytes to the output identity (P1).** `score` digests `--model-dir` and refuses to run unless it matches `NEMOTRON_88K.model_sha256`, once at process start rather than per shard. `score_corpus digest` prints the digest for a directory; over the deployed folded directory it reproduces the pinned `e1be09c9…`, so the check passes for the run already on disk. `--model-tag` is removed: it let the `model` column disagree with the bytes that produced the scores. The manifest is unchanged — adding a scorer-identity column would invalidate the manifest the completed run was built from, and the check belongs on the process that writes.

**Reject partially mismatched shard basename sets (P1).** The guard now runs on the complete basename sets, so an embed shard the token side does not name fails the manifest. That direction is the invisible one: rows are enumerated from the token side, so such a shard never becomes a row and its documents miss the footer totals, scoring and verification together with every remaining count staying self-consistent. The completed run has no such shard — summed embed rows equal normalize's counters exactly for all 292 sources, which is impossible if an embed shard is missing — so the stricter guard does not change that input.

**Fail instead of publishing a known-short shard (P1).** Raises before the write.

**Select the requested number of shards per source (P2)** and **propagate failures while reading normalized text (P2).** The flag selected one shard from each of N sources and never N shards; it is `--sources-per-pattern` for what it does. The read propagates — normalize, tokenize, embed and the scores are co-partitioned under one basename, so a missing text shard is a broken assumption rather than an absent optional input.

**Keep the zero-gated document token out of attention (P2).** Correct about the claim, declining it here. The deployed checkpoint has `doc_embed_super_token: true`, so any change to how that token enters attention changes the forward of the model that just scored 18,710,478,349 documents, and this PR's output has to stay reproducible from the checkpoint on disk. The finding is about exactness at initialization, where `doc_gate == 0`; in a trained checkpoint the gate is learned. It belongs with a retrain and a measured parity comparison.

🤖 Restructured around both blockers. `bucket.quality_step` is a StepSpec whose Zephyr pipeline reads the normalized shard (row order), the fusion score leaf and the content-type leaf, applies the per-type calibration, and writes `source`/`id`/`content_type`/`raw_score`/`score`/`quality_bucket` per basename in the normalized row order as a `QualityScores` artifact, so `build_clustered_store` consumes it directly. `hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity; `hero_data.fusion_scores`, `hero_data.content_type` and `hero_data.harrier` register the pinned inputs and the manifest carries all four stages for the 292 sources. `score_fusion.fusion_score_step` replaces the score_corpus CLI as the raw-score producer: one Zephyr task per shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the normalized text through the tokenize stage's core. The Nemotron tokenize leaves the August run read are no longer on S3, so that run's scores are registered by path rather than rescored; the smoke on nsf_awards ran both stages on the cluster.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: [grug] Separate model and data fast tracks
topics.body:
* keep the model track on `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` and add two independent Zephyr data tracks
* for a new dataset, sample the Hero production mixture from `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` and its pinned `datakit/store_4d2e363d` source store
  * preserve seeded component loader order and retokenize with `hero-bpe-v16384`
  * set fraction `p` of the final training mix to new data
  * scale the existing Hero weights by `1 - p`.
  * require the available token count. Reuse one bounded Hugging Face prefix across scales and simulate the production epoch count.
  * do not apply topic or quality classifiers to this track.
* for quality experiments, sample raw text from all 292 registered DataKit sources in proportion to available corpus size, without topic clusters or Hero mixture weights
  * reject missing source pins. Use a seeded cyclic interval in the document-ID hash space and omit only row groups with proven-disjoint ID statistics.
  * this is a hash-interval sample; document inclusion events are not independent Bernoulli draws.
  * each ladder rung specifies a model size and training-token budget. Prepare 174,787,133,440 raw tokens for the largest 17,478,713,344-token MoE rung.
  * prepare features and scores for the 174,787,133,440-token raw pool once. Reuse those scores across smaller rungs.
  * for separately prepared features, require independent expected normalized-text and Harrier-output paths for every raw source, with exact agreement between the pins and the prepared artifact.
  * at each rung, take a prefix from the fixed, seeded random document order, with ten times that rung's training budget. Reject constant candidate or incumbent scores within that prefix and preserve the original document locators.
  * rank documents by classifier score. Select documents from the highest scores until their token total fills the training budget.
  * fit a ridge head to frozen GLM quality targets and cached Harrier features.
  * exclude every document ID from the original GLM label export, including IDs without joined features. Also exclude duplicate groups from joined label text.
  * for repeated document IDs with identical text and targets, keep the first embedding in sorted path/row order. Record vector differences in a content-hashed report.
  * choose `features`, `score`, `select`, or `train` with `--stage`. Use `--scored-pool` for reuse and `--moe` for MoE models. Reject options that the selected stage cannot use.
* keep the DataKit workflow available through `uv run fast-track --source-mode sample`.
* the earlier dense Hero-mix pilot completed three matched d512 baseline/treatment seed pairs at 361,758,720 tokens per run.
  * BPB means bits per byte. Higher BPB is worse
  * a rebuild under the long-string policy preserved all 52,746 WikiText rows and 4,194,501 tokens in exact order.
  * a 10% WikiText mixture did not improve the Paloma or Uncheatable macro score in these three pairs. No larger rung started.
  * at seed 0, a 99% mixture increased Paloma BPB from 1.5290 to 2.8578 and Uncheatable BPB from 1.2353 to 2.5097.
  * these disposable probes use assumed production counts of 10B total tokens and 100M available new-dataset tokens. They do not establish production dataset value.
* the real GLM/Harrier probe froze 79,335 labeled documents and fit a ridge head with development MSE 0.03946
  * a separate calculation reproduced all scores in the 307-document integration pool
* the earlier four-source quality pilot prepared 6,064,023 documents and 3,617,587,227 tokens from `cp/arxiv_abstracts`, `cp/wikiteam`, `docx-corpus/en`, and `starcoder2/documentation`
  * ridge scores ranged from 0.0244 to 1.0080, with low-score withdrawal notices and damaged pages as well as technical text in the private document sample
  * matched dense d512 seed-0 runs each used 361,758,720 tokens, the same model configuration, and unchanged evaluation sets
  * quality-selected versus random-selection Paloma macro BPB: 1.9051 versus 1.6164. Uncheatable: 1.5914 versus 1.3522
  * 20 of 23 dataset metrics were worse after quality selection. No larger rung started
  * one-seed, four-source pilot only. Selection also changes source and length distributions. Evaluation text overlap remains unaudited
  * [quality-selected run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft9371-quality-ridge4-candidate-d512-s0-20261004) and [random control](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft9371-quality-ridge4-random-d512-s0-20261004) both succeeded

* use `fast-track-long-string-v1` for Hugging Face and raw-corpus tokenization
  * use the production tokenizer's 10,000-character split mechanism to bound long-string encoding
  * preserve full text and document identity. Token IDs can change at split boundaries.
  * bound text batches and reject a sampled document above 64 MiB with document context. Do not drop or truncate it.
  * bound native tokenizer batches without changing the existing text split points. Keep native batch behavior for padding and stochastic BPE configurations.
  * a local 32 MiB sampler probe preserved all 19,532,169 token IDs. Bounded native batches reduced peak RSS from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB.
  * synthetic short-document batches took 4–8% more time in three-repeat median comparisons. These measurements do not establish production throughput.
  * the first four-source preparation exceeded an 8 GiB worker limit. Its replacement stopped on two 38 MB documents above the previous 32 MiB document limit.
  * the two real documents passed exact-token comparisons at 2.31 and 2.40 GiB peak RSS. Four synthetic 64 MiB cases stayed below 4.86 GiB peak RSS.
  * a document one byte above 64 MiB failed with source and document context. The corrected preparation and matched training pilot succeeded
* bound pending token-cache buffers by bytes and document count while preserving token order and cache metadata
  * one `cw-us-east-02a` 6,350-document prefix benchmark reduced median cache-write time from 6.24 seconds to 0.773 seconds, with identical ordered token hashes
  * this measures one 4,194,548-token prefix, not full-pipeline throughput. The largest measured RSS was about 899 MiB
* the final focused suite passed all 92 fast-track and disposable Focus-feature tests; required lint and type checks passed
  * the full affected suite had 6,043 passes and 18 failures. One changed CLI test read the wrong nested trainer field; it passed after that assertion was corrected.
  * fresh serial checks found ten current passes, including the corrected CLI test. Five storage failures matched the clean baseline and passed on both checkouts with local scratch storage.
  * one C++ reward mismatch and two 60-second JAX timeouts also occurred on clean baseline `6940dbb764856c9b286eac3b800e3fa36b0753a0`. No branch-only failure was found. The timeouts remain unresolved.
  * no numerical tolerance, marker, or per-test timeout changed
* four-scale MoE validation is in progress at d512, d768, d1024, and d1280
  * reuse one completed maximum Hero sample and one completed WikiText prefix. The disposable exposure probes declare 20B production tokens and 100M available new-dataset tokens.
  * the d512 Hero baseline, 10% WikiText mix, and 99% WikiText mix each completed at 1,250,426,880 tokens. At seed 0, both mixtures worsened all 23 dataset BPB scores.
  * versus Hero, the 10% mix increased Paloma macro BPB by 4.07% and Uncheatable macro BPB by 1.97%; the 99% mix increased them by 58.98% and 72.54%.
  * the d768 Hero baseline completed at 3,633,315,840 tokens. The remaining matched comparisons are not complete.
  * one d768 99% launch stopped during W&B setup because its command omitted offline mode. The failed run is retained; it is not a dataset-quality result.
  * a [CPU-node incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/607) caused Iris to retry both d1024 parents and restart their GPU children from zero. Checkpoint saving was disabled; no manual restart was made.
  * the all-292-source raw quality pool is still in preparation. Its quality-training comparisons have not started.
  * these single-seed checks do not establish a production-data improvement. Experiment scripts remain outside the branch.

The following DataKit design and experiment record precedes the separate Hero-mix and quality tracks. The DataKit sample target is 25B input tokens across all 292 registered sources, with corpus-size sampling weights recorded in its completion manifest. Training rejects a store with fewer usable tokens than the requested budget. The ladder includes model widths of 512, 768, 1024, and 1280, each with dense and MoE variants. The largest default ladder run requires 17,478,713,344 usable tokens.

Run source-recipe, embedding, quality, assignment, and centroid-sampling drivers in the pipeline coordinator with up to 64 concurrent steps. The 292-source registry graph has one remote artifact-step job instead of 879. Moving those source drivers from remote jobs to the coordinator preserves all 2,477 artifact identities.

Centroid training remains remote. Within each DataKit fast-track run, all Zephyr stages share one worker with 120 CPUs, 1900 GiB RAM, and 25 TiB disk, without GPU reservation. This profile reserves about 94% each of the allocatable CPU, RAM, and disk capacity on an RNO2A H100 node. Registry-mode download and normalization also use this pool. Tasks retain their resource requests, with CPU and RAM admission limits. Model training uses a separate 8-H100 job.

The Zephyr coordinator permits 68 concurrent pipelines and uses 100 RPC threads. Fray passes actor concurrency to Iris through the fix from [PR #8497](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8497). The previous 32-thread limit let pipeline waits block worker heartbeats.

JAX coordinator names include the full child job token and attempt number. This prevents a training job from connecting to another child job’s JAX coordinator. The sibling naming approach comes from [PR #8941](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8941). This change retains the existing attempt isolation.

The data artifact path includes the terminal DataKit store identity and tokenizer vocabulary size. Runs with the same recipe and version reuse that artifact, independent of their training run IDs. Changes to source recipes, tokenizer identity, or cluster configuration select a different artifact path. Set a new `fast-track --version` to rebuild the outer artifact while retaining unchanged upstream caches.

The sample builder writes its completion record after every source succeeds. `--source-mode cache` selects the existing `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` cache.

DataKit drivers install CPU dependencies. GPU setup reinstalls the installed CUDA toolchain version when its `ptxas` binary is missing. Artifact loading restores absolute bucket paths. Disabled W&B mode reaches the GPU tasks.

The negative control reads a completed baseline store and shuffles ordinary tokens within each document. Document order, lengths, token counts, and special-token positions stay unchanged.

DataKit groups documents by content cluster and quality range. Each bucket can contain documents from several sources. Training samples each bucket in proportion to its token count. It uses training seed 0 and the same [ladder model and budget defaults](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/rav/e2e-data/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py) as the baseline. Evaluation data stays unchanged.

The [25B sample job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Ffast-track-sample-25b-20261002) succeeded in 9 minutes 37 seconds. Its verified manifest contains all 292 sources and their sampling weights. The sample occupies 34.6 GiB.

The completed store contains 29,858,746,027 usable tokens across 39 buckets and 18,236,230 documents across all 40 buckets. One bucket has only 974 tokens, below the 4,096-token training sequence length. The usable-token count sums all tokens in buckets with at least one full sequence. It does not round each bucket down to full sequences.

The store source list matches the sample manifest. The store occupies 37.3 GiB and exceeds the largest ladder budget. The 25B sampling target estimates input size, so it differs from the measured token count.

The initial data attempt used four Iris jobs: the pipeline coordinator, Zephyr coordinator, one worker, and centroid training. No per-source driver jobs appeared. It failed after 2 hours 24 minutes during large-cluster counting. Arrow changed the count column to nullable after aggregation, which prevented the next merge. The correction restores the declared schema after each aggregation.

The recovery reused completed stages and finished the data store in about 45 minutes, with three data jobs. The cached centroid model removed the separate centroid-training job from the recovery. The two attempts used seven data jobs in total.

Available Finelog samples cover each data worker attempt on `cw-rno2a`. The node agent samples task containers about once per minute. CPU values are means of snapshots, and RAM values are the largest sampled working sets. Times below are UTC on October 3, 2026.

| Worker attempt | Sample interval | Samples | Mean CPU cores | Largest sampled RAM (GiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Initial DataKit attempt | 02:29–04:50 | 137 | 104.63 | 207.52 |
| Cached DataKit recovery | 06:07–06:48 | 42 | 5.28 | 43.09 |
| Token shuffle | 06:51–08:20 | 89 | 0.84 | 55.21 |

The initial pipeline coordinator averaged 0.05 CPU cores across 143 samples. Its Zephyr coordinator averaged 0.02 across 141 samples. The initial worker requested 1 TiB each of RAM and disk. Recovery and shuffle workers used the 1900 GiB RAM and 25 TiB disk profile. Full-node reservation did not produce sustained full-node CPU use during recovery or token shuffling. Kubernetes task telemetry does not measure disk use.

These experiments used the implementation through `d3a6671929`, before the later model/data-track changes. All eight baseline runs trained on the unshuffled completed DataKit store and succeeded on October 3, 2026. Each completed run has final evaluation metrics and a permanent checkpoint at its requested training budget. Callback steps start at zero, so the final checkpoint step is one greater than the callback step. BPB means bits per byte. Each macro score is an unweighted mean across the evaluation suite’s dataset tags with observed tokens.

| Baseline | Training tokens | Paloma macro BPB | Uncheatable macro BPB | Checkpoint step |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [d512 dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d512-dense) | 361,758,720 | 1.5345 | 1.2554 | 690 |
| [d512 MoE](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d512-moe) | 1,250,426,880 | 1.3241 | 1.0166 | 2,385 |
| [d768 dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d768-dense) | 1,069,547,520 | 1.3750 | 1.0715 | 2,040 |
| [d768 MoE](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d768-moe) | 3,633,315,840 | 1.2067 | 0.8925 | 6,930 |
| [d1024 dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d1024-dense) | 2,894,069,760 | 1.2635 | 0.9517 | 2,760 |
| [d1024 MoE](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d1024-moe) | 9,720,299,520 | 1.1077 | 0.7950 | 9,270 |
| [d1280 dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d1280-dense) | 5,230,297,088 | 1.1980 | 0.8868 | 4,988 |
| [d1280 MoE](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d1280-moe) | 17,478,713,344 | 1.0573 | 0.7448 | 16,669 |

The [ladder coordinator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-ladder-retry1-coord) permits two training jobs at the same time. The coordinator and its training jobs succeeded. The initial d768 dense run succeeded after two automatic retries. Those retries exposed the sibling JAX endpoint collision. The current coordinator uses the corrected endpoint names and retains completed results.

At 10:41 UTC, Kueue preempted the ladder coordinator to admit another workload. Iris retried the parent and recreated its two active training jobs. Completed baseline artifacts remained cached. The d1024 MoE run restored its hourly resume checkpoint at step 4,843. The d1280 MoE run restarted from zero because its first hourly checkpoint was not yet due.

The two runs later completed at their full budgets. The final d1280 MoE attempt took about 9 hours 57 minutes, including evaluation and checkpoint saves.

The 25B validation used 28 distinct Iris job IDs. This count includes the sample job, the two negative-control attempts, and earlier failed or stopped jobs. The count includes six root coordinators, fourteen model-training jobs, three Zephyr coordinators, three Zephyr workers, one centroid-training job, and the sample job. No per-source driver jobs appear. Parent retries can recreate children under the same IDs, so this count does not include every execution attempt.

The [negative-control coordinator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d512-negative-retry1-coord) and its two training jobs succeeded. The controls reused one completed shuffled store with all 40 bucket counts unchanged. Their model, optimizer, training seed, token budget, mixture weights, and evaluation data match the corresponding baselines. Permanent checkpoints record steps 690 and 2,385. The initial control coordinator completed the shuffle, then failed at GPU initialization because it used the earlier JAX endpoint names. The corrected coordinator reused that store without new Zephyr jobs.

| d512 model | Paloma baseline → shuffled BPB | Uncheatable baseline → shuffled BPB |
|---|---:|---:|
| [dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d512-dense-negative) | 1.5345 → 2.8840 (+88.0%) | 1.2554 → 2.7451 (+118.7%) |
| [MoE](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-testbed-25b-20261002-rno-d512-moe-negative) | 1.3241 → 2.8311 (+113.8%) | 1.0166 → 2.6906 (+164.7%) |

Higher BPB is worse. The two controls show worse evaluation after within-document token shuffling. These comparisons use one seed and do not estimate variation across seeds.

For the experiment implementation through `d3a6671929`, lint and type checks passed. The affected suite had 5,940 passes, 156 skips, 6 expected failures, and one native-proxy HTTP 502 failure. The same proxy test also failed on main. The cluster-count regression reproduced the live schema failure before the correction. All 21 focused cluster-planning and text tests passed after the correction.

The JAX regression reproduced the sibling collision before the endpoint correction. All 29 JAX initialization tests passed after it. Source-driver execution, cache reuse, and the worker resource correction also passed their focused tests.

topics.title: [inference] Cover June Snowball TPU parity
topics.body:

TPU vLLM at TP8 serves the same checkpoint's BF16 export and records all 64 responses before applying the measured probability bounds through 32K. The four H100 cells remain. All six use Iris interactive priority.

The native cell restores checkpoint arrays directly into the BF16 exemplar dtype through Marin's TensorStore staging and replica path, avoiding a transient FP32 device copy on v6e-8. The GPU FA4 checkpoint golden and 64-prompt fixture remain intact. TPU vLLM bounds are measured compatibility ceilings, not exact numerical parity; #7555 tracks remaining long-context differences.

This focused port supersedes #7556's parity changes. topics.title: [inference] Keep Snowball serving axes on mesh
topics.body:
## Summary

Keep size-one `expert` and `context` axes on Levanter's inference mesh. Snowball's explicit partition specs name these axes even on a single-axis serving slice. Without them, the first forward pass fails with `Resource axis: expert ... is not found in mesh` after the 67B export loads.

## Validation

- `tests/inference/test_serve.py -k inference_mesh`: 3 passed.
- Project changed-file lint and type checks passed.
- The June Snowball 67B exported-checkpoint H100 parity cell passed all 64 representative prompts with this exact patch applied in #9400's then-head `8f6f28c63c`; maximum probability error was 0.056754 against the existing 0.075 bound.

This small backend fix is the base for the focused TPU parity PR #9400. It does not change the checkpoint, prompts, or numerical bounds.

The temporary pin is #27 head `5fe2ea21172a628331b732ea89f95cdd918fd398`, stacked on #26. The paired vLLM SHA and upstream-base metadata stay fixed. The generated runtime requirement follows the descriptor. This PR is stacked on serving-mesh fix #9401; focused parity PR #9400 is stacked here.

[Native Levanter on TPU](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fsnowball-tpu-checkpoint-b94f709f) also matched the frozen top-25 golden exactly at that head. The four H100 cells passed too. Generated dependency and lock checks, changed-file lint and type checks, seven descriptor tests, and fork #27 lint and CPU checks pass. This PR remains draft until fork fixes #26/#27 merge.
