🤖 **On partial key offset and MLA absorption:** it stays compatible. The KV cache is unchanged, and only the absorbed QK product widens.

- **Our MLA key:** per head h, the key is `k_{j,h} = W_uk,h · c_j`, with `c_j = RMSNorm(x_j W_dkv)` the cached latent. (The k-side short conv is off in this config: `sconv_sites=attn,mlp`.)
- **The offset** takes the first half of each head's key channels from the previous token: `k_{j,h} = [W_uk,h^A c_{j−1} ; W_uk,h^B c_j]`, where A/B are the first and second halves of W_uk,h's output columns, and the A half is zeroed at a document start.
- **The score still absorbs**, now into two latent-space queries:
  `q_h · k_{j,h} = (W_uk,h^Aᵀ q_h^A) · c_{j−1} + (W_uk,h^Bᵀ q_h^B) · c_j = q̃^A_h · c_{j−1} + q̃^B_h · c_j`.
- **What it costs at inference:**
  - The cache still stores only `c_j`. `c_{j−1}` is the previous row of the same cache, so it needs no extra storage, and in a tiled kernel it is one extra row per KV tile.
  - The QK dot is over 2 × kv_latent instead of kv_latent. Equivalently, the kernel treats the cache as `[c_{j−1} ; c_j]` against `[q̃^A ; q̃^B]`.
  - The document-start mask zeroes the `c_{j−1}` term for the first key of each document; for a single-document decode, that is just j = 0.
  - Values and the W_uv absorption are unchanged.
- **Other terms:** the Inkling relative bias, qk_mult and SSMax (if kept) act on q or on the logits, not on the cached latent, so they don't interact with this.
- **Results so far:** −0.0061 / −0.0116 on two seeds at d512 (batch 44). It is in the stacked run in batch 48.

**The fixed-time exchange rate is steep.** From the fit, `L − 1.2 ∝ C^(−0.0865)` with `L − 1.2 ≈ 1.86`, so 1% fewer steps costs about +0.0016 loss.
- 1M ×10 is 9.2% slower than the base, costing about +0.015. That leaves roughly **−0.007** at fixed time.
- 524k ×10 is 4.8% slower, costing about +0.008. That also leaves roughly **−0.007**.

So at fixed time the extra rows don't pay for their speed cost unless the table's gather/scatter gets cheaper. Batch 51 runs the 524k ×10 stacks at fixed time to check this estimate directly.

**Stack with bg 1M ×10: 3.0240, −0.0351 at equal steps**, the best so far (the 524k/×1 stack was −0.0310). It runs at 620 ex/s, 21% under the base's 785. By the exchange rate above, that costs about +0.038, which would put it roughly even at fixed time. The batch-51 fixed-time runs measure this directly. At d512, throughput is now the binding constraint on the stack: the ReLU² top-12 dispatch and the bigram table's gather/scatter.

🤖 **Batch 51: the stack at fixed time** (d512; vs soft-cap 10 = 3.0591 at 2817 steps / 785 ex/s = 8 min)

At equal steps, the stack is now at **−0.0310**: bg + ungated-kernel relu2 + ema + key offset (batch 48). ReLU² at 576 experts / top-12 still costs ex/s (638 vs 785), because top-12 routing moves 1.5× as many tokens through dispatch. So these runs take the 8-minute budget, with steps = 2817 × (run ex/s) / 785, to see what survives at fixed time. Both stacks also carry the batch-40 finding (bigram table LR ×10) and MuonEq per-input (−0.002 / −0.004).
- **full:** bg 524k ×10 + relu2 + ema + key offset + MuonEq, at 638 ex/s → **2289 steps**.
- **no-relu2:** bg 524k ×10 + ema + key offset + MuonEq, at about 745 ex/s → **2673 steps**. The same stack also runs at 2817 steps, to separate its ML gain from its speed cost.
- **base at 90% of steps:** measures the loss per 1% of steps directly. So far I have estimated it from the compute-scaling exponent (about +0.0016 per 1%), and that estimate decides whether the slower changes pay at fixed time.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **fixed time**: full stack | [`15f5f9cfc8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/15f5f9cfc8) | [lc1-b51-ft-full](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b51-ft-full) | 2289 | 635 | 3.3396 | 3.0643 | +0.0052 vs 3.0591 |
| **fixed time**: stack without relu2 | [`15f5f9cfc8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/15f5f9cfc8) | [lc1-b51-ft-norelu](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b51-ft-norelu) | 2673 | 731 | 3.3103 | 3.0414 | −0.0177 vs 3.0591 |
| equal steps: stack without relu2 | [`15f5f9cfc8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/15f5f9cfc8) | [lc1-b51-eq-norelu](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b51-eq-norelu) | 2817 | 744 | 3.2981 | 3.0325 | −0.0266 vs 3.0591 |
| base (soft-cap 10) at **90% steps**: measures the step exchange rate | [`15f5f9cfc8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/15f5f9cfc8) | [lc1-b51-base-90pct](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b51-base-90pct) | 2535 | 784 | 3.3582 | 3.0763 | +0.0172 vs 3.0591 |

**Result: ReLU² 576/12 doesn't pay at fixed time, and the stack without it is the new d512 candidate.**

| run | steps | ex/s | final (EMA) | best blend | Δ vs 3.0591 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| full stack, fixed time | 2289 | 635 | 3.0643 | 3.0604 (0.5) | **+0.0052** (blend +0.0013) |
| no-relu2 stack, fixed time | 2673 | 731 | 3.0414 | 3.0395 (0.75) | **−0.0177** (blend −0.0196) |
| no-relu2 stack, equal steps | 2817 | 744 | 3.0325 | | −0.0266 |

- **The measured exchange rate agrees with the estimate.** The no-relu2 stack loses 0.0089 going from 2817 to 2673 steps (−5.1%), about **0.0017 per 1% of steps**, against the +0.0016 estimated from the scaling exponent. The base at 90% of its steps is still running as an independent check.
- **ReLU² 576/12:** it is −0.009 at equal steps but 19% slower, which is worth about +0.03. It is out of the fixed-time recipe until its dispatch cost drops.
- **d512 candidate:**
  - the recipe
  - soft-cap 10
  - a bigram 524k table (AttnRes source, table LR ×10)
  - weight EMA (β 0.995, last 1000 steps, blend 0.5–0.75)
  - MLA partial key offset
  - MuonEq per-input

  At fixed time it gives **−0.018 / −0.020 with blend**, i.e. a compute multiplier of about **1.13×** over the soft-cap-10 base (`k = (1.8591/1.8395)^(1/0.0865)`).
- **What's next:** the bigram table is the remaining speed cost (731 vs 785 ex/s, −7%, worth about 0.012). Its dense gradient is a 0.5 GB `psum` per step, plus Adam over 268M replicated parameters. Batch 52 tries a low-rank table (width 128 / 256 with a shared up-projection) that cuts both costs by 4× / 2×.

**Exchange-rate check: the base at 90% of its steps (2535) gives 3.0763, +0.0172**, i.e. **0.0017 per 1% of steps**. This is independent of the stack's 5% point, which gave the same slope, and it matches the scaling-exponent estimate (0.0016). Rule of thumb at d512 for fixed time: **1% of ex/s ≈ 0.0017 loss.** A change is worth keeping only if its equal-step gain exceeds 0.0017 × its percent slowdown.

topics.title: [multimodality] Integrating Vision with Marin Delphi Architecture Experiment
topics.body:
# Description 

This issue tracks tracks the initial exploration at integrating a vision encoder and projection with the Delphi language only base model that Marin has already trained with the goal of extending this to omnimodal capability.
We leverage the prior work done on baseline VLM training with Qwen3 1.7B and 4B language model backbones. 

# Results

# References

-  #2383
- [Qwen 3.8 Omni](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.25611)
- [SmolVLA](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01844)

comments.body:
# Evaluation strategy
The first thing to establish are some useful evals to measure the performance of the Marin based VLM. Previously in #2383 the following benchmarks were used and scores achieved. 


Benchmark | Score
-- | --
MMMU | 46.7
ChartQA | 75.6
MMStar | 58.1
OCRBench | 68.8
RealWorldQA | 70.6
SeedBench | 76.2
ScienceQA | 89.6


This result was obtained using a [three stage training approach](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/2383#issuecomment-4130294651): 

| Stage | Goal | Data | What's Trained |
|-------|------|------|----------------|
| **Stage 1 — Language-Image Alignment** | Align vision encoder feature space with LLM embedding space | LLaVA-558K image-caption pairs | MLP projector only (vision encoder & LLM frozen) |
| **Stage 1.5 — High-Quality Knowledge Learning** | Inject broad visual knowledge before instruction tuning | LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-Mid-Training-85M (concept-balanced image-caption pairs from COYO-700M, Obelics, DataComp1B, LAION, ImageNet-21K, SAM-1B, etc.) | Full parameter training |
| **Stage 2 — Visual Instruction Tuning** | Teach the model to follow complex visual instructions across diverse multimodal tasks | LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-Instruct (~22M samples, 124 task types) + FineVision | Full parameter training |

Our first experiments will test the architecture we plan to merge in the PR, which will aim to quantify some of the basic behavior/tensor flow before we move to the next step of type of scaling behavior in typical Marin fashion. 

There are some design questions we can investigate to deepen understanding: 

1. What's the best size of the projector? 
2. How to weight the tokens between language and visual? 
3. Delphi uses the Qwen tokenizer, do we need to adapt a new one to incorporate images? 
4. How does loss correlate to benchmark performance?

Basic architecture is this, validated on some data from LLAVA 558K ```mermaid flowchart LR n1[SigLip] --> n2[Projector] --> n3[Delphi 998M] n4[Text Processor] --> n3[Delphi 998M] ``` Setting up training with another experiment for larger run.

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

Two BFCL tasks fail at startup across the Grug and Qwen runs I checked: `bfcl-simple-javascript-7` and `bfcl-simple-javascript-42` both exit 127 with `pi: command not found`. Examples from your campaign: [Grug](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20260929-233116-open-athena-Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21-bfclparity-pi-dace) and [Qwen](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20260930-084341-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-bfclparity-pi-8288). (Saw the same failures while rerunning for new models, then checked these original artifacts.)

Figuring out the root cause, then will submit a stacked PR here with the fix!

🤖 Removed checks that grepped timeout constants from source code, corrected the stale Gemma reference, used the concrete completion response type, and replaced weak resume/startup coverage. The resume test now checks the persisted result path and an unchanged scored-zero trial; the startup test observes the configured timeout inside a real child process.

The review also identified a separate Sotopia limitation: its native episode runner ignores the declared input-token budget. The campaign README, YAML, and PR description now state that those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy. Request-boundary enforcement for Sotopia remains follow-up work under #9566; the new Mini-SWE guard applies only to SWE-bench.

🤖 Removed the Marin Sotopia and Mini-SWE wrappers and their harness dependencies. The campaign now uses the native Harbor agents, pinned to `94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe`.

The standalone Harbor PRs are merged, with required CI green:

- [#231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231) packages Sotopia and classifies judge failures as verifier infrastructure errors.
- [#232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) enforces Mini-SWE's total-context budget using the serving tokenizer, including the chat template and tools.
- [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233) loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before overrides and uses its batch agent. Context exhaustion saves the trajectory without an interactive prompt, allowing Harbor to verify the existing patch.

Live checks launched through Marin:

| Check | Harbor revision | Scored | Runtime errors | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIME smoke | `d6ed12671a16` | 8/8 | 0 | Mean reward 0 |
| Sotopia | `d6ed12671a16` | 1/1 | 0 | Mean reward 0.5 |
| SWE-bench Verified | `94b118022fe3` | 1/1 | 0 | Mean reward 0; clean `ContextLimit` exit |

The final Mini-SWE trajectory contains 126 responses with reported token usage. The largest prompt plus reply was 32,377 tokens, below the 32,768-token limit; the largest reply was 1,016 tokens, below the configured 1,024-token cap. Harbor ran the verifier on the saved patch after the context-limit exit. These small-model smoke checks validate runtime behavior, not benchmark accuracy.

The saved records are:

- AIME: `gs://marin-eval-metadata/evals/20261003-022202-qwen3-0.6b-aime-smoke-6fd7/record.json`
- Sotopia: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-022258-qwen-qwen3-0.6b-native-sotopia-20261003-8234/record.json`

Marin CI completed successfully with 51 checks observed and none failing or pending. Local validation passed: 2,421 affected safe tests and 273 evaluation tests, plus lint, type, lock, and generated-pin checks. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget; those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K policy.

<summary>Advisory review response</summary>

The advisory pass prompted two documentation fixes: template kwargs accept booleans or strings, and resume checks bind the model, judge, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit before submission and again on the worker.

I retained build_evaluation_batch as the launch composition point; object-store resume validation is already delegated to validate_harbor_resume_root. The S3 client still binds the supplied temporary credentials when constructing the cached client, and HEAD and GET retain their operation-specific wrappers around the shared retry_with_backoff implementation. The thinking-policy test builds real evaluation batches with conflicting model defaults and verifies the resulting request options; it protects the policy-over-model precedence at that boundary.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

comments.body: great! minimal speed difference. I am hoping the total grad norm can start arching downwards before we make the swap, but probably fine either way.

I think swap to 16k context length will make the most sense, since its similar speed at 4k. Then when we want to do the first cooldown we can jump to 65k, another 4x gain. 4x jump per extension is on the more conservative side in literature. So I don't think we need to stick with 2x. Then another 4x to 262k at the very end of training.

On the 67B MoE we saw context extension 8k->65k at 20 percent into the run occur fine, with a grad spike in the first 10 steps but no loss spike. So it should be fine to swap when LR is still higher at 50 percent into the run.

The decision point during the swap is how we modify qk_mult. I think it is worth trying a couple options for 100 steps each w/ an eval at the end of each to empirically inform the decision. Deepseek empirically found their own optimal coef for MLA. The options are 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1) -> 1.48, or 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1)^2 -> 1.68, or we take the midpoint at 1.58. Then we with whichever shows the lowest paloma macro and uncheatable eval loss. 

It is a little surprising that the total grad norm hasn't started going down on the hero run at 47 percent in. Though it looks stable enough to not be concerning. - if we were to see substantial continual grad norm rise after swap during 100 step test, then we could consider holding off on context extension until LR is at lower position 60-80 percent into the run.

The main reason for doing the context length increase now instead of later would be to enable the earlier cooldown to have a longer window at higher context, which is particularly relevant because the current plan is to use that earlier cooldown for RL'ing experts for the first pass of the final model.

When we change context length, we will have to be careful to make sure that every other schedule in the model still works correctly. The LR schedule, the weight decay schedule, the data mix schedule, the eval schedule, and the metrics around run_progress, and tokens_consumed.

🤖 Context-switch inventory, independently audited across data/resume, schedules/model settings, and eval/metrics against `main` at `3daf065582`. This revises the earlier inventory: **constant tokens per update preserves the schedules, but does not preserve the exact data stream**. The list below states implementation requirements and deployment prerequisites. The implementation is in draft PR [#9639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9639), rebuilt as three commits after independent xhigh code review and lint review; no review findings remain. Formatting/type checks pass, 135 targeted tests pass, and 2,901 selected tests pass. Twelve selected-suite failures and one focused checkpoint timeout reproduce on the base revision. Accelerator rehearsal and live cutover have not been performed.

**Schedules and model configuration**

- Keep the production update at **46,137,344 tokens**: batch 11264 at 4096, 5632 at 8192, or 2816 at 16384. Pass the actual context into both the model and optimizer heuristic. This preserves the 390251-step schedule, MuonH/Adam learning rates, beta2, epsilon, warmup/decay/cooldown fractions, and gate/router weight-decay annealing. Changing only batch or only the model silently changes these quantities. The weight-decay schedule reads the restored Adam count; restore the full optimizer state.
- Preserve the existing zero-based `run_progress = global_step / 390251` convention. Bounded diagnostics currently use their early stop as the denominator; fix them to use the full schedule. Grafana ETA depends on the existing convention. Watch, GC, eval, and checkpoint step cadences remain valid at constant tokens/update; checkpoint wall-clock cadence still follows elapsed time.
- Make context length, QK multiplier, and receiver capacity explicit launch settings. The current QK scalar applies to both local and global layers. The discussion proposes 16K trials at approximately 1.48, 1.58, and 1.68; choosing a winner requires evaluation. Global-only scaling would be an additional model change, not an existing option. Do not hardcode unmeasured QK/capacity choices into a phase table.
- Model and optimizer arrays have no batch/context-shaped leaves. Restore uses the new static model configuration with the old parameter/optimizer arrays and counters. A real save/resume rehearsal must still exercise the new compiled shapes, expert routing, and attention kernels. Local RoPE remains at the 2048 window; longer global attention changes FLOPs and memory.

**Data order and resume**

- The loader has no checkpointed cursor: it seeks by global step and batch schedule. Use a constant new sequence batch on relaunch. A historical sequence-batch schedule mixing 4K and 16K units does not represent token history correctly. Rebuild the datasets and loader at the new context length.
- Set `BlockShuffleConfig(io_block_size=2**20 // seq_len, window_blocks=512, perm_type="feistel")` for the Harrier mixture. It matches the old default at 4K and preserves the outer permutation of 1Mi-token blocks and complete 512Mi-token windows at longer contexts. **It does not preserve within-window order.** Keep the seed, component order, immutable token store, and shuffle policy fixed.
- The previous 17B-token estimate was a simulation result, not a general repeat bound. Each of 200 cells can have an in-progress 512Mi-token window: their combined window size is about 107.4B tokens. Per-cell mixture cursor shifts and truncated dataset tails are separate effects. The earlier naive-relaunch estimates (2.85T repeated and 1.6T unique tokens missed) have not been independently reproduced; use them as motivation, not a correctness guarantee.
- **Retain the 49152-sequence mixture blocks.** Shrinking them with context length changes floor-rounded per-cell weights and the remainder assigned to the largest cell. A calculation with the checked-in weights at step 195125 gives about 108.9B tokens of aggregate absolute complete-block cursor shift at 16K if the blocks are shrunk.
- With unchanged mixture blocks, the main/cooldown stage starts are 108000/312192 at 4K and 8K, 108096/312192 at 16K, and 108288/311808 at 64K. The previous inventory estimated 2.95B tokens of aggregate per-cell cursor displacement for the 4K→16K change with unchanged mixture blocks and the 108000→108096 historical boundary; that numerical estimate has not been independently reproduced. Require explicit acceptance when a continuation shifts these boundaries. Do not assert identical per-cell token blocks in the acceptance gate.

**Metrics and evaluation**

- `throughput/total_tokens` remains exact at the same completed step when tokens/update stays fixed. A one-rack rehearsal using fewer actual tokens/update has different data offsets and cumulative tokens even if its optimizer uses the production token budget.
- Cumulative `total_gflops` currently reprices all past updates using the new context. Supply a verified cumulative-FLOP baseline at the completed handoff step; add the new phase's cost after that boundary, retaining the baseline on retries. At boundary N, use the parent total after N completed updates (normally logged at global step N−1). Per-step MFU should use the new FLOP cost; compare speed using tokens/s and elapsed iteration time.
- Pin canonical `eval_dropless/*` evaluation to **4K packing** so inherited parent rows and the `eval_regressed` alert compare the same packing. Run 16K evaluation under a distinct prefix in the trial. Fixed packing does not isolate the effect of training context when QK also changes: record QK and use matched-QK controls when attributing gains.
- Run evaluation after the first resumed update, with deduplication when the periodic/final hook hits the same step. The old first-step hook fires only at global update 1, otherwise the first new-context evaluation can wait until the next 3000-step boundary. Dropless evaluation must emit the watchdog's evaluation lifecycle events. Rehearse train → eval → next train, including dropless memory, before deployment.

**Rehearsal and acceptance**

1. CPU regression checks: compare 4K/8K/16K schedules and optimizer updates from restored counters; verify constant token totals, fixed shuffle-window coverage, documented mixture boundaries, fixed eval packing, resumed eval cadence, and cumulative FLOPs across retry. Exact optimizer/schedule equality is appropriate; exact shuffled batches and equal loss are not.
2. Restore the actual handoff checkpoint on one rack: use a 4K/QK1.3 control and 16K arms at QK1.48,1.58,1.68, each for 2–3 seeds × 200 steps. Add 4K controls at matching QK values if attributing a gain specifically to training context. Use `schedule_steps=390251`, production optimizer tokens/update, and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The original diagnostics used a smaller optimizer budget and zero gate/router decay. Smaller execution batches still change gradient statistics and data position; this is a rehearsal, not a production-equivalent gradient comparison.
3. Measure loss offset/drift, grad norm, router/drop metrics, tokens/s, iteration time, and peak memory. Include a dropless evaluation at each required packing and a save/resume. Record replacement acceptance/rollback thresholds for loss drift, gradient spikes, expert drops, throughput, and memory from these arms before authorizing deployment. The earlier measured context-dependent loss offsets mean the normal same-objective paired-loss gate cannot be applied unchanged.
4. During the production trial, verify LR, Adam LR, progress, token totals, mixture stage/weights, and FLOP continuity at matching completed steps. Compare windowed loss/gradient/drop/throughput statistics with the rehearsal bands. Score parent and child checkpoints on fixed held-out Paloma and uncheatable sets at both packings; keep short-context retention and long-context quality separate.

**Handoff record and remaining decisions**

Update the run ID, complete durable checkpoint, W&B fork point, source SHA, context/batch/QK/capacity, eval policy, FLOP baseline, mixture-shift acceptance, and rollback command together. The trigger should validate the child tracker has the same settings on retries and record them in #8506. Check checkpoint metadata, region-local storage headroom, and retention before the cutover. An old binary without requested permanent saves needs a forced temporary checkpoint copied to a durable prefix before pruning; each full hero copy was estimated at 4.29 TB in the earlier inventory. The previous live step/ETA is stale and must be refreshed at deployment.

Open deployment decisions: final QK and capacity, explicit acceptance of the 16K data shift, empirical trial thresholds, and the handoff checkpoint/time. A 64K or 262K phase also needs its own batch/mesh/attention and memory validation. The changes described here do not establish those later deployments as ready.

> Wonder if its possible to do a clean handoff point as long as our checkpoint lands on a step that is divisible by the right number.

@ClassicLarry I've been looking into this, and it seems pretty tricky to resume with a different context length without repeating or dropping tokens. It seems like there are at least 4 independent sources of potential misalignment:

1. Levanter currently splits sources into "shuffle blocks" of 256 sequences and then the blocks are permuted. When we change the sequence length, the block sizes also change and the permuted sequence differs. So even if we restart the run at a shuffle block boundary, we'll inevitably drop and repeat tokens. #9689 fixes this by setting the tokens per shuffle block to ~1M (the current value, with 4k context), independently of the context size.
2. In addition to the block-level permutation above, we also permute _sequences_ within 512-block windows. When we change the sequence length, we change the result of permutation. (Note, we can't just work around this by doing the handoff at a step divisible by some number, since each source is at a different point in its window, and the rate at which tokens are consumed from a source is determined by its mixture weight). This seems like the largest effect after (1) and also the hardest to work around.
3. The token stream is divided into "mixture blocks" of 49152 sequences. To avoid dropping/repeating tokens, we need to hand off at a mixture block boundary. For a given batch size, mixture block boundaries coincide with steps every `49152 / gcd(49152, B)` steps. At C=16k, B=2816, this is 192 steps.
4. The data mix has a stage start at 108k. But mixture stages must fall on steps that are also mixture block boundaries, which are multiples of 192 steps at batch size 2816 (what we'd use with 16k context). We could either move the stage start to 108096 or 107904; the former skips some tokens from sources whose weight decreased at the switch and repeats some tokens from sources whose weight increased; the latter vice-versa.

One option is to merge #9689 to fix (1), hand off at the 216k permanent checkpoint to avoid (3), and accept the drops/repeats due to (2) and (4). I'm a bit hesitant, though - it seems like this has the potential to drop/repeat 10s of billions of tokens.

Wondering if we should instead look into an adhoc patch, something like finishing each source's current window in the order the 4k run was using before switching to 16k? This seems like it could get quite messy, though, and I'm hesitant to pursue it unless we think it's really necessary.

@ravwojdyla @Helw150 curious for your thoughts here as well. How did we manage this for the 67B run?

🤖 **Proposal: a clean context-length handoff** (replying to @mcwitt's four misalignment points above)

1. Fix shuffle blocks at ~1M tokens, so the level-1 block permutation is the same at every seq_len (#9689).
2. Give each data-mix stage its own `seq_len` and `batch_size`, e.g. `(216000, mix2, seq_len=16384, B=2816)`. A stage then only has to land on a mixture-block boundary in its own units, which fixes points 3 and 4.
3. Track each source's read position in **tokens** carried across stages, instead of in sequences of a single length.
4. On a `seq_len` change, advance each source to its next shuffle-window boundary (skip-to-window). Nothing repeats; only the unread rest of each source's current window is skipped, which fixes point 2. Using `harrier_mix_2026_08_18` at a 216k handoff, that is about **52B unseen tokens** across 200 sources, ≈0.26B each and ~0.6% of the remaining run.
5. Inside a stage, mixing, batching and BOS/EOS/segment handling are unchanged.

Finishing the partially read windows instead would serve leftover 4k slices glued into 16k sequences. Those need segment and loss masking at the joins, carry only 4k of context, and low-weight sources would keep serving them for thousands of steps after the switch. So skip-to-window looks like the better trade-off.

Thanks for the thorough investigation! The 67B would have had some reshuffling on its context length change, I did not account for all levels of the shuffle there.

I am in favor of skipping ahead to each data bucket's next 512-block window. So at most a data bucket will skip 512x256x4096 = 500 million tokens. I cant think of a clean way around this.

In the future a solution might be to not permute sequences in step 2, and instead only permute at max_seq_len, where max_seq_len is based on what we will eventually use in the training run.

We will face this challenge again when we go to 65k. So perhaps we should have the code permute sequences at 65k now, then chop up at 16k.
Wondering what Rav and Will think here. Would defer to them on what we think will minimize impact.

For the hero, we already shuffled the data globally in Datakit, so we could keep a fixed token-sized I/O block shuffle and drop the inner sequence shuffle. That'll make our shuffle logic context size independent for the rest of the run (and I agree skip the rest of the current block for everything here).

🤖 Re-run of this experiment on the hero MoE optimization stack (#9829–#9834, now deployed as `hero-mfu30-step231k`). 8K and 16K still train, the stack speeds up every length by about 10%, and the long-context costs above still hold.

Setup: same as above (one GB200 NVL72 rack, restore `step-180000`, steps 180000–180099, 4,194,304 tokens per step, qk_mult 1.3/1.39/1.48), seed 0 only. Every arm ran on the same rack (DH1-138), and each stack/pre-stack pair ran back to back. Pre-stack is main `3a955d678e`, the commit before #9829; the stack is `a9b3cb8167` (#9834 head). Statistics cover steps 180011–180099 without the profiled steps 180021–180023.

| Arm | Code | Step time | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak HBM | Drop fraction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | pre-stack | 13.97 s | 300.3k | 28.11% | 115.5 GiB | 1.71e-4 |
| 4K | stack | 12.70 s | 330.3k | 30.91% | 124.0 GiB | 1.88e-4 |
| 8K | pre-stack | 14.18 s | 295.8k | 28.36% | 115.5 GiB | 8.31e-4 |
| 8K | stack | 12.89 s | 325.5k | 31.20% | 124.0 GiB | 8.46e-4 |
| 16K | pre-stack | 14.41 s | 291.0k | 29.23% | 115.5 GiB | 3.15e-3 |
| 16K | stack | 13.15 s | 319.0k | 32.03% | 123.4 GiB | 3.14e-3 |

* The stack saves about 1.27 s per step at every length (+10.0%, +10.0%, +9.6% tokens/s), and the extra time for long context is unchanged: 16K adds 0.449 s over 4K with the stack and 0.446 s without. As a fraction of the shorter step, 16K costs 3.4% of 4K throughput with the stack against 3.1% without.
* Drop fractions at 8K and 16K are unchanged by the stack (paired ratios 1.02 and 0.99). The 4K drop fraction varies by up to 6.5% between identical reruns, so the 4K difference is noise.
* Peak HBM is 123–124 GiB with the stack at every length, against a 143.8 GiB allocator limit. topics.title: [grug] Add GB200 launch and H100 validation support
topics.body:
Stack the GB200 launcher, checkpoint/data support and H100 validation runner on the pipeline foundation in #9279 for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. It requests one hard NVLink domain in the opportunistic BATCH queue and separates queue wait from worker execution deadlines. Future run names use `pipeline-gb200-*` or `pipeline-h100-*`.

Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 synthetic gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. No checkpoint was written in those full-width trials. Save/restore support is included, but hardware checkpoint validation is limited to the historical reduced-model comparison: a 90,018,826-byte scratch checkpoint and a resumed-versus-uninterrupted loss difference of 9.5367431640625e-7, within unchanged 1e-5 tolerances. The current full-width main-recipe checkpoint path has not been validated on GPUs. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Main-recipe argument parsing rejects AdamW before distributed initialization. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

#9279 contains the shared expert-bank normalization correction, FP32 main-recipe precision and optional frozen QB bias, together with their CPU regressions and historical layout explanation. The hardware gates used FP32 parameters and BF16 compute, with per-expert normalization and adaptive QB. They do not validate the shared-bank normalization correction or frozen-QB mode.

The combined executable, runtime and test source is identical to the previously published `5c2d91a6e48a43573b7f0b09be7e5f16bfc3eddc` snapshot. The README now selects per-expert normalization explicitly in its historical reproduction command. Required lint, type checks, hooks, strict docs and source-link checks passed on that source. The affected safe suite passed 5,566 tests with 18 skips and six expected failures, using library imports from the current checkout. Focused CPU coverage passed 81 tests; the previous normalization fails the new layout regression. The committed-branch lint-catalog review completed; the new error-wording assertion finding was fixed. Before merge, #9279 owns the named compiled-initializer result, repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers and synthetic runner lifecycle cleanup. This extension then owns adapting its checkpoint/data lifecycle. Those deferred changes need compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation.

Full 48-layer main-recipe execution remains unvalidated. The 64-GB200 rack attempt acquired its allocation and started some native processes, then failed during runtime installation; it produced no finite training updates. The full 192-H100/48-layer/65K run remains held. This pull request remains draft.

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher takes --seq-len and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit --qk-mult, applied to all attention layers; --capacity-factor overrides the expert receiver capacity. A resume at a new context also requires --context-switch-step and --flops-baseline-step/--flops-baseline-total. The new prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config turns the switch step into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with the Harrier stage schedule at the 4K batch size and the 4K shuffle blocks, so the Harrier sources continue from their 4K reads. Hero eval stays at 4K packing. A context switch is rejected for runs below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff, because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache.

trigger_hero.sh records the context, batch, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and context switch step in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh still launches at 4K. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Stacked on #9890, which is stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/585) matches two empty `/silo/<id>` cgroups to Silo shims, but nested containerd's completed-container inventory and the failing cleanup path remain unverified. The Silo pod is still running; this checkout has no Silo implementation to patch. No overlapping open PR was found.

**Relevant code and evidence**
- [`tasks.py#L2654`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2654) — Iris builds the workload pod.
- [`tasks.py#L2588`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2588) — exec path for a running task.
- [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/585) — host counts and sampled shim IDs.

# Proposed Fix

1. With @muchanem, identify the deployed Silo revision and its source. Inventory nested containerd namespaces, completed tasks and containers, shim PIDs, and their `/silo/<id>` cgroups; determine which IDs persist after container exit and deletion.
2. Trace those IDs through Silo's task deletion, container deletion, and shim reaping paths. Add a failing lifecycle test for the observed exit path, fix the responsible cleanup path in Silo's source, and cover cancellation if it follows a separate path.
3. Repeatedly create and tear down containers with the affected configuration. After each batch and its cleanup grace period, verify that completed tasks, shim processes, and `/silo` cgroups return to baseline.
4. Coordinate a targeted recovery of `g5bc6da` with the pipeline owner only after stale IDs are reconciled with containerd state. Recheck cgroup counts and confirm that a new Kubernetes pod starts; an empty `cgroup.procs` alone is insufficient grounds for removal.

🤖 Silo's sandbox deletion leaked every gVisor (`runsc`) sandbox. All Silo hosts are now stopped and their leaked cgroups removed. Silo stays down until a host with the fix is deployed.

**Cause**

Silo deletes a sandbox with `nerdctl rm -f`. Under `runsc`, nerdctl 2.1.2 kills the sandbox and then tries to delete the task. The delete kills again, `runsc kill` fails with "sandbox is not running", and nerdctl exits 0 anyway. The stopped task, its `containerd-shim`, and its `/silo/<id>` cgroup stay. Silo saw exit 0 and counted the sandbox as deleted.

Reproduced on `cap-pipeline-host-53` (2026-10-04): the same `nerdctl run` then `rm -f` removes everything with `runc`. With `runsc` it exits 0, and the container, its `STOPPED` task, its shim and its empty cgroup remain. The leaked containers carried the label `nerdctl/error: unknown error after kill: runsc did not terminate successfully: exit status 128: sandbox is not running`. Host-53's nested containerd held 19,415 such containers.

**Fix**

`NerdctlRuntime.remove` now checks containerd after `nerdctl rm -f`. If the container is still there, it runs `ctr task delete` (no kill, since the task is already stopped) and then `ctr container delete`. About 0.2% of leaked containers also had `runsc` state that still said "running" for a dead sandbox, and their task delete was refused. For those, `remove` runs `runsc delete --force` first. If the container still cannot be deleted, `remove` raises: the sandbox stays `destroying` and the host's reaper retries it. On host-53, both steps removed the shim and the cgroup. A regression test covers both cases. The fix is on the `mark/silo` branch and is not yet pushed.

**Cleanup (owner-run, 2026-10-04 ~23:05–23:45 UTC)**

All hosts were idle (0 running sandboxes) during the cleanup.

1. On each of the 17 `cap-pipeline-host-*` pods on cw-us-east-02a, I deleted every container with a `STOPPED` task through that host's own containerd, using the sequence above. Live sandbox tasks are `RUNNING`, so they were not touched.
2. I then removed `/silo/<id>` cgroups that were empty, older than 30 minutes, and unknown to that host's containerd.

The node-wide memory `num_cgroups` count fell from 10K–35K to 700–1,250 on 15 nodes. I then cancelled all 17 hosts. The 3 `cap-rno` hosts on cw-rno2a had no leaked containers in their containerd; the sweep removed 10,481 orphaned cgroups on one node and 510 on the other, and those hosts are cancelled too. The `cap-pipeline` broker is still running; it creates no cgroups.

**Not resolved**

- I could not finish two cw-us-east-02a nodes before cancelling. Their empty `/silo` cgroups remain until the cleanup script runs or the node reboots:
  - the node of `cap-pipeline-host-52`, about 33K at the start, where exec stopped responding;
  - the node of `cap-pipeline-host-47`, about 4.3K, where the cleanup was still running.
- About 1–2 containers per host had a zombie sandbox process, and `runsc delete --force` hangs on them. Cancelling the pod clears them. With the fix, `remove` times out after 300 s, logs the failure, and retries on the next reap.
- The cw-rno2a node of `cap-rno-host-4`/`-9` still reports about 12K memory cgroups, but 11,958 of them are dying cgroups (deleted, still pinned by page cache). The kernel frees these as the cache is reclaimed.
- Repeated create and teardown on a deployed host with the fix has not been run yet. It will be checked on the first host brought back, by watching memory `num_cgroups` and the shim count.

topics.title: Share Hero and Snowball checkpoint export mechanics
topics.body:
Share bounded HF shard-writing code between Hero and the Levanter converter used by Snowball. Hero reuses the converter's 5 GB file planner; a source tensor larger than that target remains whole. Local files are written directly, while remote files stage under `TMPDIR` before upload.

All JAX ranks replicate tensors in matching order. Only process zero copies weights to CPU and writes files. One writer process supports host-local paths and existing HF upload callbacks. An `ExitStack` owns each memory reservation during gathering; successful submission transfers cleanup to the shard-write task's completion callback. Process zero broadcasts writer failures at matching checks on all ranks.

Hero resume verifies the export request identity and shard checksums before reuse. It writes `export-manifest.json` after all shards and HF metadata to mark completion.

CPU export checks cover exact Hero/Snowball weights, concurrent uploads and two-rank failure/recovery. Full-size accelerator exports and live cloud/HF uploads remain untested.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent. Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that motivated this check is recorded in the [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

🤖 Rebased #9721 onto `origin/main` (`974a9ae152`); the branch now points to [`b77ac3f4bc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/b77ac3f4bc2deb5f38558aeadb66b4a83e106730). The two conflicts combined independent test additions and imports. GitHub reports the PR mergeable, and CI has restarted. The focused Iris suite passed (61 tests), as did lint and type checks. The broader safe suite had 4,973 passes and three SkyRL launcher failures: their separate `uv` project could not install `langdetect` because a directory in the shared uv cache was missing. The failure reproduces before the launcher code loads.

I would keep this opt-in check in Iris for now. Iris already deploys a node-local agent, supplies the task storage environment, and owns the controller action that stops new placement on a bad node. If we add several fleet-wide probes or need the same policy for workloads outside Iris, I would move both the probe DaemonSet and its single cordon decision-maker into a fleet-health operator. Kubernetes [uses DaemonSets for node-local monitoring](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/) and [Node Problem Detector supports custom checks](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/monitor-node-health/); its condition/event reporting would still need our peer comparison and cordon budget policy.

For this workload, the probe should exercise the same regional endpoint, credentials, and network path as a task; use a hard deadline, small scratch object, and lifecycle expiry; and classify configuration failures separately from node-local transport failures. Keep the quarantine decision on fresh per-node evidence with a persistent streak, healthy-peer majority, cordon budget, and manual recovery. Export result, latency, and report age to the monitoring pipeline for trends and alerts; the current PR persists the latest evidence in node annotations and logs. Kubernetes [describes metrics as a separate scrape and time-series pipeline](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/observability/).

Before enabling automatic cordons, I would run with `max_cordoned_nodes: 0` and confirm the probe detects the affected task path. The current node-agent DaemonSet uses `hostNetwork: true`, while task pods use pod networking by default, so a pod-network-only fault could be missed. The [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599) showed `Ready` and generic node checks staying healthy while storage requests failed; moving the task off the node restored training, but it did not prove every storage error shares that cause.

My recommendation is to keep the Iris-owned probe in this PR while validating it in observation mode. Do you want that scope, or should I prepare a separate fleet-health operator before this PR merges?

comments.body:
🤖 Updated [PR #9721](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9721) through [`54958cdeac`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/54958cdeaceae70a8cf9e46f39fe6c0d08ce6996) and addressed the review threads, recovery blocker, and documentation nit.

`kubernetes_provider.node_health` now groups the storage check and shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under separate one-day TTL scratch prefixes. After a fresh successful probe for the current node and configured target that started after the cordon, the controller removes an Iris-owned cordon and releases its budget, including after reboot or credential rotation. The node-agent DaemonSet already tolerates cordons, so it continues probing; operator cordons without the Iris annotation remain. The CoreWeave guide and PR description reflect this behavior. These are config changes; no live cluster was restarted or deployed in this session.

Validation: 70 focused Iris tests passed; changed-file lint, format, YAML, Pyrefly, and strict MkDocs checks passed. The affected safe suite had 4,978 passes, 7 skips, 6 expected failures, and three SkyRL launcher failures. Those three reproduce before the launcher imports because the isolated `uv` project cannot read a missing `langdetect` directory in the shared cache. CI passed on the latest commit (45 checks observed). The PR is approved and mergeable.

The [IaC preview](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9721#issuecomment-6042860044) shows the expected Nodes `patch` RBAC grant for CoreWeave. It also shows IAM member removals and a binding deletion in the separate `marin` stack. This branch does not edit IAM declarations; that global-stack preview needs separate review before any apply.

🤖 **Blocker: an automatic cordon can get stuck, and it then holds the full cordon budget.**

To release a cordon, `reconcile_storage_health` must get a healthy report with the same node UID, boot ID, and target as the cordon report ([storage_health.py#L206-L212](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04b76b9324c8457a31d0db6bd3d5eeb726531d8b/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/storage_health.py#L206-L212)). The `reboot` case of `test_recovery_requires_fresh_matching_node_probe` makes sure that a rebooted node stays cordoned. Two usual events cause this:

* **Reboot.** A reboot is the most probable repair for a node-local storage fault. After the reboot, the node probes as healthy but it stays cordoned.
* **Credential or endpoint change.** `target_id` includes `environment_revision`, and the deployment calculates that value from the `iris-task-env` Secret `resourceVersion`. `_s3_task_env()` reads the credentials from the shell of the operator who deploys. Thus a key rotation, or a deployment with different keys, changes the target. After that change, the controller cannot release the cordons that it made before.

The three production configs set `max_cordoned_nodes: 1`. Thus one stuck cordon stops all quarantine on that cluster, and no signal shows it. Each time, an operator must uncordon the node and remove the annotation.

Recommended change:

* To release a cordon, accept a fresh healthy `current_report` for the node that started after the cordon report. Do not compare the UID, boot ID, or target to the cordon. `current_report` already rejects a report that is stale or that has the wrong target.
* Keep the incarnation and target fence only for peer evidence. If the controller compares `peer.target == report.target` directly (and each agent hashes its own endpoint, credential key ID, and scratch path), the PR does not need the `environment_revision` config field or the Secret read and `model_copy` sequence in `start_controller`.

🤖 Fixed the recovery blocker in [`3a6abb1af0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/3a6abb1af0089f162120e2bf075f5132be6594b9). An Iris cordon now releases after a fresh healthy report for the current node and configured target, started after the cordon report. It no longer requires the old UID, boot ID, or target to match. Reboot, node replacement, and environment-rotation regressions pass (70 focused Iris tests); lint and type checks pass. The environment revision remains because it rolls agents on Secret rotation and fences peer evidence from different credentials.

topics.title: [inference] Adopt GPU releases with one wheel pin update
topics.body:
Document source approval on marin-community/vllm's main before the fork
builds, qualifies and publishes GPU wheels. Test the published wheels in a
Marin adoption PR by comparing Snowball token probabilities with stored
references. Root agent guides and refresh automation point to this order and
its automatic/manual test table.

Render generated dependencies before changing gpu.toml so rendering failures
leave existing pins untouched. Future refreshes replay Marin's fork patches
from fetched fork main, retaining patches landed before wheel adoption.
Preserve current dependency checks, production pins and dependency targets.

Supersedes #9397's staged wheel pin and later promotion proposal. The companion
workflow in marin-community/vllm#85 replaces marin-community/vllm#76. All 9
affected tests and the strict documentation build pass. The developer selecting
new wheels runs live Snowball validation before adoption.

Part of #9300
