topics.title: Hero Run: Sudden drop in PTB Paloma Eval
topics.body: Issue to track the investigation into the sudden drop in PTB Paloma Eval PTB is in general OOD data due to token, 'N' token, and all lowercase. Among other quirks. Initial hypothesises: 1. Some in-context learning capacity turned on for a checkpoint. 2. Data contam/very similar article in training data around then. 3. Some very rare tokens in PTB happened to get upweighted on a checkpoint that under normal checkpoints are heavily penalized. 4. Other/Unk Artifact comparing first 4k tokens: https://claude.ai/artifact/W82uDiQuQygwAaqfX3hEiR Most noteworthy drop is: "los angeles financier marvin" " mar" for marvin is predicted with 80% confidence on the overperforming checkpoint- seems likely that the exact phrase los angeles financier marvin appeared in the training data. It then dropped back down to its usual 0.2% on the following checkpoint. Completions API with prompt for every checkpoint: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/hero-completions/latest/index.html#a=1ed4a3edd3645961c051e72c8b85a9ec7b6fbea0f2c5b3a27960cc1c806b237d&b=dde26b9fe079446f0c76ecc1b7f469d59815aca5f3f3c84f50a3993df7a26978&prompt=biocorpus-protein-design-heldout

comments.body: 'mar' was at 15% on checkpoint 198k. And the model always knows mar ->vin ->d ->avis. So the person marvin davis is cleanly in the training data for a while. Google search-> "Marvin Davis was a prominent Beverly Hills billionaire, oil tycoon, and corporate buyout artist who made massive waves as Wall Street's highest-paid financier in 1989." Any docs related to news ongoings in Los Angeles may be spiking the eval.

PTB is '1989 Wall Street Journal (WSJ) articles'. We want our model to understand what happened in the 1980s in general.. so having the facts of this eval in the training data is intentional. Will see what comes up from scanning our data in this 6k step range.

🤖 **Data scan result: PTB's own text was in the training stream ~500 steps before the 210k checkpoint (hypothesis 2, contamination).**

**Method.** I rebuilt the hero's exact training stream from the run's logged data config: launch commit `ad754c6d67`, seed 0, the 0 / 108,000 / 312,192 mix stages, and the block shuffle. Then I read every sequence trained in steps **204,000–216,000**: 12,000 steps × 11,264 sequences × 4,096 tokens, about 554B tokens over 48 CPU jobs on cw-us-east-02a. The scan searched for PTB-specific lowercase phrases, their normal-cased counterparts, and runs of ` <unk>`.

**Result.** A block of about **231 sequences (~1M tokens)** in source **`c13q3`** at **steps 209,272–209,669** contains Penn Treebank text expanded into sliding n-gram windows (`<s> <s> … <word>` per line). It reads like an NLP exercise repository: it also has NMT training notes and scraped request headers. It includes the exact sentences in our PTB eval, e.g. `los angeles financier marvin`, `in london british airways chairman lord king`, `the stock of ual corp. continued`, `the dow industrials were off N points`. A related source, `c28q1`, has n-gram log-probability tables over the same text around step 206.3k (`lg P(corp. | acquire ual)`).

| Lowercase PTB-format hits | steps 204k–210k | steps 210k–216k |
|---|---|---|
| `los angeles financier` | 3 | 0 |
| `british airways chairman` | 3 | 0 |
| `ual corp` | 26 | 0 |

Normal-cased news about the same entities appears about equally in both ranges:

| Normal-cased hits | steps 204k–210k | steps 210k–216k |
|---|---|---|
| `Marvin Davis` | 331 | 332 |
| `UAL Corp` | 226 | 230 |
| `British Airways chairman` | 25 | 27 |

So general knowledge of the 1989 story is steady. What changed before 210k is exposure to the PTB text itself, which the checkpoint partly retained and which had faded by 216k. "Lord King" alone produced thousands of false positives ("Sovereign Lord King James…"), so those hits are excluded.

**300-character chunks: PTB eval text vs. the training document**

PTB (Paloma `ptb` val):
```
this is a total <unk> for takeover-stock traders one investment banker said 
 los angeles financier marvin davis who put united in play with a $ N billion bid two months ago last night <unk> both a ray of hope and an extra element of uncertainty by saying he remains interested in acquiring ual 
 but
```
Training stream (`c13q3`, step 209,550):
```
 traders one investment
for takeover-stock traders one investment banker
takeover-stock traders one investment banker said
<s> <s> <s> <s> <s> los
<s> <s> <s> <s> los angeles
<s> <s> <s> los angeles financier
<s> <s> los angeles financier marvin
<s> los angeles financier <NAME>
los angeles financier
```

PTB:
```
in london british airways chairman lord king was quoted in the times as declaring he is not prepared to take my shareholders into a <unk> deal 
 observers said it appeared that british air was angered at the way the bid has <unk> into confusion as well as by the banks ' effort to round up financing 
```
Training stream (`c13q3`, step 209,665):
```
<s> <s> <s> <s> in london
<s> <s> <s> in london british
<s> <s> in london british airways
<s> in london british airways chairman
in london british airways chairman lord
london british airways chairman lord king
british airways chairman lord king was
airways chairman lord king was quoted
chairman lor
```

The training copy has "marvin davis" replaced with `<NAME>` in most windows, presumably by PII scrubbing. One window, `los angeles financier marvin`, kept the first name because the scrubber only caught "marvin davis" as a pair. That is the token the 210k checkpoint predicted at 0.80. It also explains why every checkpoint already completes `marvin → davis`: that part is general knowledge, not this document.

**Takeaways**
- The 210k drop in PTB loss (about −0.2 nats, spread across almost every line) comes from verbatim exposure to the eval text in an n-gram layout roughly 330–730 steps earlier. It is not a capability change. 210k still misses PTB's genuinely surprising words ("declaring", "my"), which fits brief, partial exposure.
- Paloma PTB is contaminated in the hero mix, at least in `c13q3` and `c28q1`. Its curve will spike whenever those windows come up in the data order, so it shouldn't be read as a quality signal. Wikitext-103 and the other public eval sets may warrant the same scan.

Raw hits: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/larry/scratch/hero_scan/full/*.jsonl`. Scanner: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/scan_training_data.py` on local branch `hero-data-scan`, not pushed.

🤖 **The contaminated document, and every step that reads it**

**What it is.** One GitHub repository dump in source `c13q3`, **`quanpn90/torch-nplm`**: a Torch implementation of Bengio et al. (2003), with the name scrubbed to `<NAME>` in the README. It is **1,385,899 tokens** (4.83M characters), a single BOS…EOS document that spans 340 training sequences of 4,096 tokens.

| File | Characters |
|---|---|
| README.md | 260 |
| extract_ngrams.py | 2,308 |
| train.lua | 12,261 |
| **data/ptb/test.6grams** | **2,543,118** |
| **data/ptb/valid.6grams** | **2,262,165** |
| util/BatchLoader.lua | 4,901 |
| util/IdentityLinear.lua | 985 |

About 99.6% of the document is the **full PTB test and validation sets as sliding 6-gram windows**. `valid.6grams` starts `<s> <s> <s> <s> <s> consumers / … / consumers may want to move their / may want to move their telephones …`, which is exactly the start of Paloma's `ptb` eval document. So the whole Paloma PTB eval set is in the training data, with each word appearing in 6 overlapping windows.

First 500 characters:
```
Repository: quanpn90/torch-nplm

File: README.md
# torch-nplm

Neural probabilistic language model (<NAME>, 2003) implemented in Torch.

GPU supported for fast training.

Hierarchical supported for fast softmax-ing on a large vocabulary. 

HSM borrowed from https://github.com/yoonkim/lstm-char-cnn


File: extract_ngrams.py
#!/usr/bin/python
import sys

# This script extracts n-grams from a set of PREPROCESSED text files (train, set, valid)

data_dir = sys.argv[1]
ngram_order = int(sys.argv[2])

tra
```

**Every step that reads it over the full 390,251-step schedule.** I inverted the mixture and block shuffle using the run's logged data config: launch commit `ad754c6d67`, seed 0, the 0 / 108,000 / 312,192 stages, and `c13q3` at 69.8M sequences per epoch. The document straddles two 256-sequence shuffle blocks, which land in different shuffle windows, so each epoch reads it in two bursts:

| Epoch | Document part | Sequences | Steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | code + first ~60% of `test.6grams` | 112 | **176,080–176,355** |
| 0 | rest of `test.6grams` + **all of `valid.6grams` (Paloma PTB)** | 228 | **209,390–209,669** |
| 1 | code + first ~60% of `test.6grams` | 112 | 327,205–327,493 *(future)* |
| 1 | rest of `test.6grams` + **all of `valid.6grams`** | 228 | **362,280–362,578** *(future)* |

**Implications**
- The 210k checkpoint was saved about 330–610 steps after the hero trained on the entire Paloma PTB eval set. That explains the drop, and its fading by 216k.
- **The PTB eval should drop again right after step ~362.3k**, when epoch 1 reaches the same block; that's in the cooldown stage. It's a useful sanity check that this explanation is right. The ~176k and ~327k bursts carry only PTB test-split text, not the Paloma eval text.
- Other copies of PTB in the mix, for example the n-gram probability tables in `c28q1` around step 206.3k, aren't covered by this mapping. A dedup or decontamination pass against Paloma would find them.

Files: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/larry/scratch/hero_scan/docs/` holds the full document text (`doc_209550_4116.txt`), `summary.json`, and `torch_nplm_steps.json`, which maps every read to its step and row. Scripts: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/{scan_training_data,find_training_doc,find_doc_steps}.py` on local branch `hero-data-scan`.
Its https://github.com/quanpn90/torch-nplm/, specifically https://github.com/quanpn90/torch-nplm/blob/master/data/ptb/valid.6grams. The sort of doc that could induce very weird repetition behavior.

@ClassicLarry, I went through the public W&B evals: all 16 Paloma and 7 Uncheatable subsets, every eval from step 2,999 to 227,999. I also ran the decon matcher on the torch-nplm files. Here are four results that may help the scan. **1. PTB has drops the torch-nplm reads don't explain** | Evals | PTB loss | Note | |---|---|---| | 101,999 → **104,999** → 107,999 | 2.143 → **1.961** → 2.109 | A one-eval drop with no mapped read nearby | | 188,999 → **191,999** | 2.115 → **2.015** | Drops 0.10 and stays below 2.08 through 227,999 | | 173,999 → **176,999** → 179,999 | 2.141 → **2.099** → 2.114 | Just after the 176,080–176,355 read, which has only the PTB *test* split | | 203,999 → **206,999** → 209,999 | 2.079 → **1.903** → 1.712 | The first half comes before the 209,390 read; it fits the `c28q1` tables at ~206.3k | The 176,999 row is a natural control. That read had PTB test text but none of the eval sentences. It moved the eval 0.029 below the average of its two neighbours, while the curve otherwise stays between 2.113 and 2.141 from 155,999 to 188,999. By the same measure, 104,999 is 0.165 below its neighbours, close to 209,999's 0.187. So I'd guess another copy of the validation text was read in steps **102,000–104,999**. If your scanner can run on that range, and on **189,000–191,999**, that would test it. **2. WikiText-103 shows the same pattern; general Wikipedia doesn't** At steps 125,999 / 128,999 / 131,999 / 134,999, `wikitext_103` reads 1.707 / **1.558** / 1.638 / 1.684. Over the same evals, `m2d2_wikipedia_unsplit` reads 1.828 / 1.827 / 1.823 / 1.824. Smaller one-sided drops recur at 137,999, 152,999, 203,999 and 212,999–215,999. None of them shows up in m2d2_wikipedia. A 0.15 drop on the WikiText eval with flat general Wikipedia looks like a document containing the eval text itself, not a Wikipedia-heavy stretch. Candidate windows: - **126,000–128,999**; - **210,000–212,999**, which your 204k–216k scan already covers. Re-running it with a few WikiText eval sentences may be the cheapest first check. **3. Decon would have missed torch-nplm even with Paloma indexed** Paloma isn't in the decon eval corpus, and `wikitext` is excluded on purpose (`DECON_EXCLUDED_EVAL_TASKS`, #6852 cluster A). I indexed the PTB validation text (Paloma's `ptb`) anyway to test the matcher. I ran the matching functions in `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py` unchanged, using the `reference_pipeline.py` settings: 13-grams, overlap ≥ 0.5, ≥ 2 matched features, paragraphs split on `\n\n`. The repo was rendered the way `stack_v3.row_to_doc` renders it. | Training document | Max overlap | Flagged | |---|---|---| | torch-nplm as trained (6-gram windows) | 0.000 | no | | the same repo plus the raw `data/ptb/valid.txt` | 1.000 | yes | | the validation set as windows of any width from 3 to 30 | ≤ 0.14 | no | A small pre-pass recovers it. When most lines of a paragraph are windows that shift by one token, stitch them back into running text, drop ``, and score the result as an extra paragraph. Overlap goes back to 1.000. In 5,724 ordinary code and text files (the Marin repo and the CPython 3.12 standard library), the pass triggered on none of 241,449 paragraphs. Details are on #6852, the issue about this matcher's recall. So one store-wide pass may be cheaper than scanning step ranges. Run decon in flag-only mode against Paloma `ptb` and `wikitext_103`, with the stitching pass, and then run `find_doc_steps.py` on what it flags. Raw copies would score about 1.0. **4. For alerts and for comparisons with the pre-registered prediction** After the 108k mix swap, PTB accounts for 50–68% of the variance in the Paloma macro's eval-to-eval movement, and WikiText-103 for 19–27%. The ranges cover three detrending methods; the block-bootstrap 95% CI for PTB is 0.33–0.85. Dropping both subsets cuts the macro's noise SD to 43–61% of its current value. The 7 Uncheatable subsets show no drops at any threshold I tried, which fits #9729. For the Paloma chart and the #8435 comparison, a 14-subset macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103`, shown next to the official one, would keep these exposures out of the trend. Scripts and outputs: [eval-audit/](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/eval-audit). Everything uses the public W&B project and public GitHub files.

topics.title: [levanter] Preserve staged mixture indices beyond 2^31
topics.body:
Staged mixtures now preserve child indices when a stage begins after 2^31 samples. Cumulative counts previously used 32-bit storage, and multiplying a stage's block count by samples per block also overflowed before accumulation. Reads in the next stage could therefore use negative child indices.

A regression reads across this boundary through `MixtureDataset.get_batch`. The selected suite reported 1,235 passes, 6 skips, and one parallel worker crash in `test_train_lm_fp8`; that test passed on its isolated rerun.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

comments.body:
🤖 Two ways a profile can break a hero run, both found on one rack while testing the stack (#9830-#9834). A production rollout needs a guard for each.

**1. XLA compile abort (fixed in a candidate plugin, not yet promoted).** With `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading` (#9831), rematerialization may offload values to host when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget. One profiled schedule overshot the budget (124.77 GiB against 114.09 GiB inside the layer loop), and remat picked an f32[] operand of an all-reduce whose start was scheduled before the loop and whose done came after it. `GetCostOfHostOffload` counts users reached through the all-reduce's alias; `OffloadInstruction` places the reload before direct users only, found none unplaced, and failed `CHECK(!place_before_list.empty())` at hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118 on every rank. The bug is unchanged on openxla/xla main and has no upstream report.
- Fix: skip candidates whose buffer `has_indirect_uses` in `GetCostOfHostOffload`, as recomputation already does. Branch `marin/remat-offload-indirect-uses` (0f6dc61dee) on marin-community/xla. A plugin built from it on Iris (`0.11.1+marin.0f6dc61dee6d`, 15 minutes) compiles the case that aborted.
- A second branch, `marin/remat-no-offload-strategy` (ff858b5447), also keeps the flag's host accounting but turns the offload strategy off. Its cost model prices host copies at HBM bandwidth. It is built but untested on the rack.

**2. Out of memory at runtime.** With the fix, the same program compiled and then failed to allocate its 143.75 GiB pool on the first step. Remat estimated the profiled schedule about 26 GiB above the unprofiled one. A near-identical program (the shared expert as two custom VJPs instead of one) trained with its own profile at 119.5 GiB peak, so this depends on the schedule. I have not traced which buffers grow.

What this adds to the done criteria: before a long run, a preflight that compiles the profiled program and runs a few steps, with a fallback to no profile when either fails. Both failures appear within minutes of start.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
This is the top of a three-PR stack. The two PRs below it prepare `ep_ring.py` so this backend can share ring's gather helpers and local assignment selection instead of copying them.

Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule and the Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Every hidden-width movement is a gather, so neither pass uses a scatter-add.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The June benchmark sets it with `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` from #9852; 1.1 gave no sender drops. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and gradients, including forced sender drops. At full shapes in bf16 the output differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative, because `ring_dedup` sums in f32. The drop rate is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. That was allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer, which also hits ring at batch 96, and #9901 fixes it with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` in the HPC Fund wrapper. We have not measured `ring_dedup` on TPU or NVIDIA.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm (base `main`). Adds the gather helpers `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows` that this backend reuses.
2. #9928 [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch). Adds `_select_local_assignments`, which this backend calls.
3. #9880 this PR (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, #9928's branch).

The timings above were measured with the ROCm routing top-k from #9889 in place. That kernel is not needed here and is being replaced by #9942. The ring column ran ring with the gather combine, which #9860 now selects with `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

Part of #9615

comments.body:
🤖 Code review

No issues found.

<!-- marin-correctness-review -->

🤖 Review notes from a walkthrough of the change. None of these block the mechanism; the rename is the main request.

**Rename the prior-phase types.** `PriorDataPhase` is easy to misread: "data" does not say which aspect of the data changed, and in the Harrier code and docs "phase" already means a mixture phase (`_SPEC.phase_weights`, the JSON `phases`, "Phase 1/2/3" in `docs/reports/hero-mixture-log.md`). A context switch can fall in the middle of a mixture phase, so the two divisions of the run need different names. Suggested names:

| Current | Suggested |
| --- | --- |
| `PriorDataPhase` | `ContextPhaseConfig` |
| `LmDataConfig.prior_phases` | `prior_context_phases` |
| `MixturePhase` | `ContextPhase` |

This follows the `FooConfig` → `Foo` pattern: `ContextPhaseConfig` declares a past context phase in steps, and `ContextPhase` is the form `skip_to_window_offsets` uses (start step, `BatchSchedule`, stages in sequence indices). The `ContextPhase` list also holds the current phase. The `MixturePhase` docstring ("A phase of the mixture for ...") should change with it, for example to "One context phase of the run, with its batch schedule and stages in sequence indices." Please also add a sentence to the field docstring that batch-size changes within one context belong in `BatchSchedule`, and that `prior_context_phases` describes earlier context lengths only.

Names and strings that follow from the rename:

- `_prior_phase_offsets` → `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, and `_prior_phase_window_tokens` → `_context_phase_window_tokens`.
- The `"prior_phases ..."` error messages and the `train_mixture` docstring.
- `"Every data phase must draw from the same sources"`, `"Data phases must start at increasing steps"`, and `"Prior phase {phase} must shuffle ..."` → "context phase".
- In `test_context_switch_data.py`: the imports, the `_phase` and `_offsets` annotations, and `test_lm_data_config_prior_phase_resumes_without_repeating_tokens`.
- In #9689: `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts`, so the stack uses one term. The context history that replaces `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` there (see my comment on #9689) can use the same name.

**Reject adjacent phases with the same sequence length.** `skip_to_window_offsets` accepts two adjacent phases with the same `seq_len`, for example a relaunch that changes only the batch size. In that case the within-window order does not change, so a source could continue at its exact position. `_next_window_start` still rounds up to the next shuffle window and discards up to one window per source (about 537M tokens per source at Harrier's settings). A check that adjacent phases differ in `seq_len` would turn that silent waste into an error. It would also make the `ContextPhase` name exact.

**Rename `counts_before` and make it block-aligned.** `counts_before` does not say what it counts; `sequence_counts_before` does. Its partial-block branch also never runs in this PR: `skip_to_window_offsets` calls it only at block boundaries (rounded up for the old phase, down for the new one). That branch returns a count, but in a partly served block the count is not a read position, because slots are shuffled; a source that served 3 sequences may have served occurrences 0, 7, and 31. Taking a block index instead, as `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, removes the branch and prevents a later caller from using a mid-block count as a position.

**Check source order across phases.** The active-source check compares sets, but order matters as much: it sets each source's shuffle key through `key_iterator`, and the mixture's slot layout through `dataset_index` (including which source receives the rounding remainder). A config that lists the same sources in a different order passes the check and gets a different data layout. Recording the source order in the prior phase and comparing lists would catch this; at minimum, the docstring should say the order must not change.

**Document two assumptions that cannot be checked here.** (1) The shuffle and mixture keys come from the trainer seed, so the seed must be the same in every phase. (2) The offsets assume the current phase starts reading at the last `end_step`. A launch that restores a checkpoint from before that step would re-read data. #9689's trigger checks this for the hero; a docstring sentence on `prior_phases` would cover other callers.

**Optional: give a prior phase a `BatchSchedule`.** `PriorDataPhase.batch_size` is an `int`, so a prior phase cannot have a batch ramp, while the current phase takes a full `BatchSchedule`. A `BatchSchedule` field would give prior and current phases one representation.

**Possible follow-up, not for this PR.** Batch-size history (`BatchSchedule`) and context-length history (`prior_phases`) are both step-indexed descriptions of the run's shape, and could become one schedule. That needs three things this PR should not take on: the trainer must reject a `seq_len` change after the current step, because `Pos` is fixed per launch, while it can follow a batch change; `BatchSchedule` is used in 28 Python files; and the Harrier stage schedule would need to record the realized step of past stage boundaries instead of rounding them again for each batch size.

🤖 Addressed in new commits on top of the reviewed head ([compare 5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/compare/5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f)):

- **Rename** (86fff8f63b): `ContextPhaseConfig`, `prior_context_phases`, `ContextPhase`, `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, `_context_phase_window_tokens`, the error messages, the `ContextPhase` docstring, and the test names. The field docstring now says that batch-size changes within one context length belong in `BatchSchedule`. In #9689, b596fe391c renames `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts` to `HarrierContextPhase` and `prior_context_phases`.
- **Same-length adjacent phases** (4ca2f1ba0d): `skip_to_window_offsets` now raises an error.
- **`counts_before`** (c7bdbe68f1): now `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, without the partial-block branch.
- **Source order** (1c99ccec06): documented, not checked. A recorded source list would not catch the case that matters: the Harrier launcher rebuilds the prior phase from the same spec at every launch, so a reordered spec changes the recorded list and the current list together.
- **Seed and restore step** (1c99ccec06): both assumptions are in the `prior_context_phases` docstring.
- **Batch schedule for a prior phase** (748ad7fe6f): `ContextPhaseConfig.batch_size` is now `int | IntSchedule`, the same type as `TrainerConfig.train_batch_size`, so the existing `BatchSchedule(...)` conversion handles both.

The unified schedule is left for a follow-up, as suggested. The `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` history from the #9689 comment is not in these commits.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost.

Stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

topics.title: [levanter] Add a benchmark for the Triton ragged_dot kernels
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which times the Triton grouped GEMM behind `haliax.nn.ragged_dot` on one GPU. For each layout (fwd, dlhs, drhs) it times both Triton kernel families (`tile_map` and `group_grid`), XLA's `ragged_dot_general` and a dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs. Each timing is the median of repeated windows after a warmup. Rows are written as JSON lines.

With `--sweep`, the script times the tile-map kernel for every block config in a bounded grid. `--shard i/n` runs every n-th config, so the GPUs of one node can split the grid. The AMD block-size table and the per-call numbers in #9859 came from this script on MI350X.

The script imports the tile-map kernels added in #9859, so this PR targets that branch. Merge #9859 first.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [haliax] Prefer XLA ragged_dot on AMD MI300X and MI325X
topics.body:
On AMD MI300X and MI325X (gfx942), `ragged_dot(implementation="auto")` now tries XLA before the Pallas Triton kernels. MI350X (gfx950), NVIDIA, TPU and CPU keep their current order. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` still overrides the choice.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X found that XLA's bf16 grouped GEMM takes 11-28% less time than the best Triton config for each fwd, dlhs and drhs triple. For example, the June w13 projection at M=131072 took 10.91 ms with XLA and 12.25 ms with tuned Triton. These numbers come from microbenchmarks only. We have not run a full-model A/B on MI300X. MI350X must keep Triton because XLA rejects bf16 `ragged_dot` on gfx950.

XLA's hipBLASLt grouped GEMM crashes with `ROCM_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when HIP command buffers are on, so ROCm runs must pass `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`. The MI300X timings above used that flag. The Grug training entry points already set it by default, and so does the HPC Fund Slurm wrapper, `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` on `main`.

`_GpuFamily` gains an `AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` member, detected from the compute capability that ROCm reports (`"gfx942"`). gfx942 keeps the tile-map kernels and the block configs swept on MI350X, so the Triton fallback is unchanged. #9905 is stacked on this PR and reuses `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` for its MI300X block configs, so merge #10009, then this PR, then #9905.

At #9905's head, which contains this PR, the file gives 46 passed and 30 skipped f32 kernel cases on MI300X (job 458222) and 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223).

Stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first, then retarget this PR to `main`.

topics.title: [haliax] Tune tile-map ragged_dot dlhs and drhs blocks for MI300X
topics.body:
Give MI300X and MI325X (gfx942) their own dlhs and drhs tile-map blocks for the Triton `ragged_dot` kernels: 128x256x32, 4 warps, 8 XCDs, group_m=2, with 2 pipeline stages for dlhs and 1 for drhs. Until now gfx942 reused the MI350X (gfx950) blocks. gfx942 has 64 KiB of LDS per CU, against 160 KiB on gfx950, and the MI350X dlhs and drhs blocks run 20-35% slower on MI300X than the swept tile. The forward pass keeps the MI350X block (256x256x64). 128x256x32 is 16% faster for fwd at the June shape with M=16384, but no faster at M=131072 and 15-22% slower at a Mixtral-like shape.

The table is keyed on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` from #9904. That PR makes `implementation="auto"` prefer XLA on gfx942, so these blocks apply when Triton is selected explicitly. Merge order: #10009, then #9904, then this PR.

The f32 skip in `test_triton_kernel_families_match_ragged_dot_general`, which #10009 adds for gfx942, now keys on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942`. Triton uses xf32 for f32 dots on gfx942, and the group-grid f32 tiles exceed the 64 KiB LDS.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X (partition `mi3001x`; jobs 454650, 454673, 454679 and 454683; sweeps 454658, 454659, 454667 and 454668) show that the tuned dlhs and drhs blocks cut a fwd+dlhs+drhs triple by 9-24%. For example, the June w13 shape at M=131072 drops from 14.67 ms to 12.25 ms.

At this branch's head, `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` gives 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223) and, on MI300X, 46 passed and 30 skipped (job 458222).

topics.title: [post-training] Compare SFT, rejection-sampled SFT and OPD transfer on Snowball with CruxEval
topics.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld. Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0).

**TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09).** Given one expert E built from the Snowball student B by SFT on GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: plain SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT), and on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts. Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. RS-SFT and OPD are both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering (1.2 / 2.7 pp) is unresolved with one run per arm and two evaluator passes. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K or MATH500. Training cost: plain SFT 61.6 H100-h, RS-SFT 57.4, OPD 376.4 for the full run (286.9 to the selected checkpoint, plus 14–15 per HF export). RS-SFT used ground-truth execution results to select demos; the other arms did not. These numbers measure transfer on seen prompts, not generalization.

**Results (selected checkpoints; CruxEval two-pass means, pass@1 %, 800 problems per direction; "gap closed" = gain over B divided by E's gain over B).**

| Model | CruxEval input | CruxEval output | Gap closed (in / out) | GSM8K | MATH500 | Training H100-h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (student) | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 | — |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — |
| E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 |
| Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 | 61.6 |
| RS-SFT on execution-correct E demos, 283 of 376 updates | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 | 57.4 (full run) |
| OPD from E, 75 of 100 updates | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 | 286.9 to the checkpoint; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export |

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`. E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2`, vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes.

**Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms).
- Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100).
- RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100).
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron).
- Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction.

**Artifacts.** Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: marin-community/skyrl run p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`, RS-SFT `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`, OPD `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`. Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<record>/record.json`.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.
- 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris.
- 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Teacher training and three transfer arms make this a gated experiment. As of 23:29 UTC, the owner has submitted the W&B-corrected teacher retry; startup, optimizer progress, and export remain unconfirmed ([latest status](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6048938002)). No open PR targets #9920, while the owner is already preparing the recipe on `task/133`; the earlier coding-teacher spike [#9528](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9528) ended without a usable MOPD transfer result.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT specification and training setup
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned SkyRL experiment and export contract
- [`experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path

# Proposed Fix

1. Follow the submitted teacher retry through a completed update, full training, and verified HF exports. Evaluate the planned exports with the frozen CruxEval/GSM8K configuration. Stop the transfer arms unless E clears the stated +10-point gate on both CruxEval directions without a GSM8K drop beyond noise.
2. Pin E, B, prompt IDs, tokenizer/template, grader, evaluator, and one eight-sample-per-prompt teacher generation artifact. Build unfiltered SFT from samples 1–4 and rejection-sampled SFT from up to four execution-correct samples. Record missing-correct-sample prompts, actual supervised tokens, and teacher-generation GPU-hours; a matched prompt set alone does not equalize training tokens.
3. Start OPD from the same B and prompts. Check teacher/student token-score alignment and one update plus export before the full run. Match the planned sweep and student update budget across arms, and record teacher-scoring GPU-hours separately.
4. Evaluate every selected arm twice with the same pinned evaluator on CruxEval input, CruxEval output, and GSM8K. Report each arm's accuracy, `(arm − B) / (E − B)` per direction, run-to-run spread, prompts and tokens consumed, and total GPU-hours. Label gains as transfer on the trained test prompts; this protocol cannot establish held-out generalization.

🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`.
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy c131e5ab, vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

topics.title: [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper
topics.body:
The next PR in this stack, #9880, adds a `ring_dedup` expert-parallel backend that selects each GPU's local expert assignments exactly the way `ring` does. This PR moves that selection into a shared helper first, so `ring_dedup` can call it instead of copying it.

`_select_local_assignments` in `ep_ring.py` covers the per-expert counts, the prefix capacity cap, the top-k selection ordered by (local expert id, flat position) and the padding of the `ragged_dot` group sizes. The computation moves without edits, so ring's behavior is unchanged. The existing ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py` pass on 8x MI350X (9 tests) and on CPU (6 tests; the 3 multi-device tests skip), in job 455432.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm (base `main`). It also edits `ep_ring.py`, so this PR sits on top of it.
2. #9928 this PR (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch)
3. #9880 [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, this PR's branch)

topics.title: [grug] Route QBRoutedMoE through the jax_triton top-k kernel
topics.body:
QBRoutedMoE now selects experts with `levanter.grug._moe.topk.top_k_indices`, called per token shard inside `shard_map`, in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. That is the jax_triton kernel from #9830, which the hero model already uses. `jax.lax.top_k` still handles rows of 1,024 or more (XLA:GPU runs its own top-k kernel on those), non-float32 inputs, non-GPU backends and environments without jax-triton.

On AMD, jax-triton 0.3.1 with triton 3.6.0, Levanter's GPU pins, compiles the kernel for ROCm with jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer. jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher, so there the kernel falls back to `jax.lax.top_k`.

Time per call in ms, from 16 calls on distinct inputs in one executable, median of 5 runs. The shapes are the router logits per call of the hero model and of the June Snowball model:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | jax_triton (this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0754 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0954 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.847 | 0.0665 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 1.000 | 0.0570 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0207 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0238 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.351 | 0.0246 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.402 | 0.0167 |

The AMD rows ran on jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0, with the AMD HPC Fund cluster's ROCm 7.2 libraries on the library path, as `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` leaves them. The `lax.top_k` baseline depends on that: with only the wheel's own ROCm libraries loaded, `lax.top_k` on MI350X takes 2.4 ms (hero) and 1.7 ms (June), while the kernel times do not change. The kernel code is unchanged since #9830; the NVIDIA rows are earlier measurements of it with the same harness.

On NVIDIA, the models that use QBRoutedMoE (`experiments/grug/moe`, `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp` and `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe`) now run the kernel, because Levanter's GPU extra installs jax-triton. In the optimized HLO of the June training step on H100 and GB200, the 4 `sort` ops of main's routing become 2 `triton_kernel_call`s, and the all-gathers, all-reduces and reduce-scatters are unchanged. Step time does not change measurably. June model at full width with 4 layers and sequence length 4096, ring expert parallelism over the node, `xla_flash` attention and XLA `ragged_dot`; median of steps 2-19 per run, runs alternating between main and this PR:

| GPU | Tokens per GPU | Runs per side | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x GB200 | 8,192 | 4 | 0.5742 s (0.5723-0.5759) | 0.5740 s (0.5719-0.5760) |
| 8x H100 | 16,384 | 5 | 1.457 s (1.403-1.508) | 1.513 s (1.336-1.539) |

On H100, step time varied between runs of the same code: main's five runs spanned 1.403-1.508 s (7%) and this PR's 1.336-1.539 s (15%). Five runs per side cannot separate the two. Scaled to these shapes, the per-call times above put the saving below 0.1% of a step. At 16,384 tokens per GPU on GB200, runs of both variants intermittently hung in a training step or ran out of memory, so those runs are left out. TPU step time was not measured; there `top_k_indices` falls back to `lax.top_k` inside the same `shard_map`.

On MI300X and MI350X the kernel's indices equal those of `lax.top_k` computed on the CPU, for widths 37 to 1,023 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently, while the kernel follows XLA:CPU and CUDA. The GPU tests therefore check the kernel's output against `lax.top_k` run on the CPU backend.

The AMD venv recipe in `experiments/amd/hpcfund/README.md` still installs jaxlib 0.11.0 without jax-triton, so runs from it silently keep `lax.top_k` until that recipe moves to 0.11.1.

Supersedes #9889, which added a separate ROCm-only Pallas kernel for power-of-two widths.

🤖 Before this merges: on AMD it will hang 8-GPU training once jax-triton is installed there, which #9989 does. `top_k_indices` launches its jax_triton kernel whenever jax-triton imports and the device is a GPU, and the June model routes through `QBRoutedMoE`. On ROCm, a jax_triton kernel fails the first time one process launches it on several GPUs at once: jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so all but one GPU fail and the step stalls at the next collective. A one-line add kernel fails this way on 8x MI350X and 8x MI325X. This top-k kernel has not run on 8 GPUs, but it goes through the same loader; the AMD numbers above are from one GPU, where nothing races. Details and a standalone repro: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9853#issuecomment-6090140907. Until AMD's jax fork fixes the race, AMD runs need either this kernel off on ROCm or one process per GPU.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launch use the carry-offload memory budget
topics.body:
`trigger_hero.sh` passed `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75` and `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=85` to the hero coordinator. Since #9831, `_apply_hero_ep_runtime_defaults` gives the hero's carry-offload configuration a 0.78 memory fraction and slop factor 105 together with `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading`. Explicit values take precedence over those defaults, and `run_grug` copies the coordinator environment into the training tasks, so a hero launched from main would compile with 0.75 / 85 and host-memory offloading on. On one GB200 rack restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint, that combination aborts compilation on every rank in `HloRematerialization` (`hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118`, `Check failed: !place_before_list.empty()`).

Without the two overrides the launch resolves to 0.78 / 105 with host-memory offloading, the configuration measured in the #9831–#9834 rack benchmarks. The live hero is unaffected: Iris retries reuse the bundle it was launched with.

Follow-up to #9831.

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.

🤖 Trinity Mini NUPA provides a child-task-level reproduction and rules out partial aggregation.

The Iris child `/benfeuer/eval-20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-a679/eval-nupa-cb8a6a13/0` has three attempts:

- Attempt 0 completed on 2026-10-02 at 06:24:54 UTC, then Iris recorded `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted` and scheduled a retry.
- Attempt 1 wrote and sealed a complete 5,000-item `NUPA5K-Loose` archive. The archive had 4,510 scored responses, 490 classified infrastructure failures, and 2,414 correct answers, so the recovered score was 2,414 / 5,000 = `0.4828`. The tracker sealed that complete attempt on 2026-10-03.
- Iris again recorded the attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` and started attempt 2 at 2026-10-03 10:41:20 UTC. Attempt 2 completed successfully on 2026-10-04 at 15:46:05 UTC and wrote `0.4788` to the same result URI.

Both reported scores cover the full 5,000-item panel. The difference is between complete replays of one stochastic evaluation under one run ID, not between a partial and final aggregate.

🤖
# Research

`build_evaluation_batch()` serializes one `run_id` and results path per evaluation. An Iris replay enters the same runner with that identity; the evaluator can reopen the sealed archive, and `write_record()` overwrites the canonical record. The September 27 and October 6 incidents document successful records replaced by retry or cancellation failures.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L213-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L213-L220) — serializes the run ID and results path
- [`runner.py#L243-L269`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L243-L269) — reuses the path and writes a record
- [`records.py#L319-L325`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L319-L325) — replaces `record.json`
- [`store.py#L175-L181`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L175-L181) — reopening clears the seal

# Attempt isolation and first-success publication

[PR #9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) already changes evaluation scheduling and uses `StepSpec` status to skip successful steps on restart. Its own description identifies the remaining crash window between writing a record and marking the step successful. This plan belongs in that PR or its successor; a separate runner PR would overlap it.

## Design

Keep the launch `run_id` as the stable tracker identity. Allocate a fresh attempt ID when an evaluation actually starts, and write Evalchemy or Harbor output, its FineStore archive, and an attempt record under `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/attempts/{attempt_id}/`. Pass that attempt's results path to the executor, so a retry cannot reopen an earlier sealed archive. Preserve the attempt ID and Iris job IDs in the attempt record for audit.

Publish `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/record.json` only after an attempt's output is sealed and its metrics are validated. Use a storage-conditional update (GCS generation or S3 ETag/create precondition) so the first successful record wins even if a lock expires or two writers race. Failure records may replace an earlier failure while no success exists; after success, later attempts cannot replace the canonical record or its referenced results. A replay that finds a canonical success should return that record path before starting serving or evaluation, including when a previous worker died after publication but before `StepSpec` wrote `SUCCESS`.

Update the launcher, runner, record writer, reporting path, and EvalDash reader together. Existing run pages keep the stable `run_id`; the canonical record points at an immutable attempt's results. Keep old flat-layout records readable for historical runs. A deliberate new evaluation gets a new launch `run_id` instead of changing an existing score.

## Costs and risks

The additional attempt directory and conditional publication path change the persistent layout and require both CoreWeave S3 and GCS semantics to be exercised. Step status and record publication can disagree after a crash; recovery must treat a canonical success as complete. Existing readers that assume results live directly under `{run_id}/results` need updating.

## Testing and completion

Add a regression that publishes a successful, sealed attempt, interrupts before step success, then replays the batch: no new evaluator runs and the canonical record and seal remain byte-for-byte unchanged. Cover failure-then-success, success-then-failure, and two competing publishers; verify that attempt records remain separate and EvalDash keeps the first successful score. Run the repository's local evaluation tests and pre-commit checks, then exercise conditional publication on the configured S3 and GCS backends before landing.

## Open question

Should the canonical path show the latest failed attempt until a success arrives, or should failed attempts appear only in the attempt history? The first option preserves current failed-run visibility; either choice must prevent a failure from replacing success.

~~On it~~ — this session was relaunched; the live status card is below.

🤖 I traced the Evalchemy revision pinned by the September evaluation policies (`c131e5ab`) and the current FineStore write path. The NUPA replay is consistent with the code: the child never restores or checks the prior durable result before starting a new evaluation.

- Evalchemy's `--resume-mode auto` looks for request state under its local `--output_path` ([resume wiring](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/wiring.py#L103-L114)). Marin creates a new `TemporaryDirectory` for that argument on every child invocation; it passes the durable result URI separately as `--finestore_output_path` ([client](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L185-L203), [task loop](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L257-L265)). Thus the retry has no local resume state. The fork opens FineStore only when writing the new aggregate and samples, then seals it ([writer](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/contracts/finestore_output.py#L32-L66)). This is an integration gap, not evidence that Evalchemy tried and failed to restore the completed archive.
- FineStore's writer deliberately clears a seal when it opens an existing archive ([DataStore](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L180-L189)). In a local two-writer check, `ReadView.is_sealed()` changed from `True` after the first seal to `False` immediately after the retry opened it. The seal describes the current archive state; it does not make the URI immutable. Marin also submits the Evalchemy child before checking existing results ([runner](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L338-L352)) and writes `record.json` with an unconditional `"w"` open ([record writer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L510-L520)).

[#9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) should skip an evaluation after its StepSpec has recorded success. Its description acknowledges the window between writing a record and marking the step successful. A child retry after sealing, or a replay in that window, can still touch the shared FineStore URI. The child needs a durable, task-specific completion check before running, with configuration and coverage validation, or a separate output URI per attempt plus protected publication of the first success. The archive seal alone is insufficient as a whole-evaluation indicator because Evalchemy seals during each task's output write, before Marin's later validation and normalization.

This conclusion is from the pinned source and a local FineStore check; I did not replay the cited S3 archive. The attempt timelines and score changes in this issue supply the production evidence.

🤖 Yes, Evalchemy can resume a partial run when it is restarted with the **same persistent `--output_path`** and a matching fingerprint. Its resume manager records each completed request or pass@k batch with enough payload to reconstruct the result, skips those units on restart, and rejects material fingerprint changes ([manager](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/manager.py#L85-L141), [restore and record](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/manager.py#L199-L243)). Marin currently gives each invocation a fresh temporary `--output_path`, so that recovery state does not survive an Iris retry ([client](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L257-L265)). Evalchemy writes native results and normalized samples to FineStore only after the evaluation completes ([FineStore output](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/contracts/finestore_output.py#L32-L66)); the current archive therefore cannot recover work lost partway through a child run.

A FineStore-backed resume store is feasible without changing the evaluator's unit-level skip/restore logic. I would make that logic persist its fingerprint and completed-unit payloads under the durable task URI using synchronous FineStore transactions, then load them through a read-only `ReadView` on retry. Commit units in bounded batches: a crash would redo at most the uncommitted batch. The normalized `samples` table is not a substitute for these payloads, which also carry the exact generation output and sample identity used to reconstruct scoring ([resume payload use](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/task.py#L390-L435)). FineStore's cache and file-set adapters are best-effort; its transactional API is the appropriate durability boundary ([FineStore docs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/README.md#L12-L43), [cache caveat](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/README.md#L122-L129)).

Recovery and final-result protection need separate checks. Read and validate a task-specific completion marker **before** opening the archive for writing, because `DataStore.open` clears an existing seal. A matching completed task should return its existing result without running Evalchemy; an incomplete task should restore committed units and continue. The completion check should include expected coverage and the dataset/task/grader revision; the [current fingerprint](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/wiring.py#L25-L35) explicitly omits controlling-file digests. Finally, protect the run-level success record from later attempts. A FineStore seal alone cannot serve as that marker: Evalchemy seals after each task's output write, before Marin finishes its validation and record publication.
