topics.title: Add aligned Snowball checkpoint merging and calibration
topics.body:
Add aligned Snowball/Grug checkpoint merging, including weighted averages, task arithmetic, TIES/DARE, RAM, expert transfer, serial merging, learned coefficients, calibrated curvature grafting and ISO composition. Source tensor names, shapes, dtypes and expert identities must already align; the tools do not infer expert permutations.

The constrained export path preserves original Base metadata, tensor layout and at least 75% of its scalar weights bit-for-bit. It reads every written object back, counts actual scalar changes and saves the successful audit outside the model directory. Both serial stages are checked against original Base. The historical unconstrained exporter remains available separately.

The [Campaign 2 README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weight-merging/public-methods-20261009/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/README.md) provides pinned parent revisions, commands to remap all 54 recipes to fresh paths, CPU/GPU and calibration requirements, and the exact BFCL/NUPA evaluation checkouts. It links all 48 completed candidates with preparation/export timing estimates and unrounded result evidence. DARE-TIES-02 scored 45.53 BFCL and 0.00 NUPA200 while changing 6.04% of Base parameters. Non-target retention was not evaluated. Historical calibration tensors and raw evaluation transcripts remain private, so refitting/rerunning is supported but exact calibrated-output replay is not guaranteed.

All 46 focused CPU tests and required formatting/type checks pass. The broader safe suite reached 2,517 passed, 13 skipped and five xfailed, with three pre-existing RL launcher failures and 15 collection errors from the unavailable Linux bubblewrap dependency. The unchanged preceding PR revision reproduces the launcher failures and the same missing dependency on representative collection paths.

Part of #9975.

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

comments.body:
🤖
## Hero figure

![Method shootout: best summed target score, unrestricted and under a common estimated merge-compute budget](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/resolve/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/method_shootout.png)

Figure 1. Retrospective comparison of 113 evaluated checkpoint variants across 11 method families. Each bar sums the NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity percentage scores of one checkpoint (range 0–200); its two segments are the two benchmark scores. Left: best observed sum in each family. Right: best observed sum in the chronological prefix that fits a common 1.0e15 estimated merge-FLOP budget per family. Trials are ordered by first evaluation submission; shared calibration and precursor exports are charged once within each family, including precursor exports from other families. No later trial is skipped ahead of an over-budget trial. Experiment counts: Serial merging 28; Activation-guided transfer 21; Layer / component merging 30; Expert Merging++ adaptation 4; Weighted averaging 5; DARE-linear 2; OTA + FFG adaptation 4; RAM / RAM+ 4; Task arithmetic 10; TIES 3; DARE-TIES 2. The 21 activation-transfer variants include five random-transfer and five recipient/metadata controls; these ten controls consume budget but are excluded from maxima in both panels. Counts represent checkpoint variants with both scores, not independent seeds or all attempted jobs. The campaign largely combined the NUPA and BFCL specialists; the best serial checkpoint copied about 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from Base, the intended recipient model. Unequal search effort and differences in tokenizer and model configuration files between checkpoints confound algorithm comparisons. Both benchmarks were optimization targets; these maxima do not establish held-out gains or general capability retention. Compute is an arithmetic estimate, not measured hardware FLOPs or total search cost: evaluation, original benchmark captures, NUPA activation collection, failed attempts, I/O and quadratic attention work are excluded. The full recorded BFCL replay corpus is charged once as shared setup to each family that uses activation-selected transfers; that replay alone costs about 3.8e16 FLOPs, so activation-dependent trials exceed the main-panel budget even with those omissions. The right panel is a retrospective budget filter over the observed trial sequence, not a prospective equal-compute experiment.

[Budget sensitivity](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/resolve/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/budget_sensitivity.png) · [Per-family scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/family_ranking.csv) · [Per-experiment data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/experiment_data.csv) · [Plot source](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/plot_shootout.py)

NUPA200 is the fixed 200-task subset of the policy's 5,000-task NUPA panel; BFCL-Parity is the `bfcl_parity@1.0` Harbor adaptation evaluated with the Pi agent: one trial for each of 123 tasks, reporting verified solve rate (mean task reward × 100), not the full BFCL leaderboard score. See the [evaluation policy release](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/RELEASE.md). Each bar selects both scores from one checkpoint. Base is Grug Antidoom Step12, NUPA is Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92, and BFCL is Grug Reference-KL Step20. The best raw sum is 85.28 for serial merging; at the illustrative 1.0e15 estimated merge-FLOP budget, layer/component merging leads at 47.40.

The archive contains the saved scores and recipe metadata needed to recreate this plot. Exact end-to-end replay is not possible from the archive alone: benchmark transcripts and tokenizer payloads were excluded, and intermediate weights and full curvature tensors were not stored locally. [Reproducibility scope and gaps](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/REPRODUCIBILITY.md).

🤖
## Parent and finalist scores

| Checkpoint | NUPA200 (%) | BFCL-Parity (%) | Sum |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base: Grug Antidoom Step12 | 0.50 | 5.70 | 6.20 |
| NUPA: Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92 | 38.00 | 16.30 | 54.30 |
| BFCL: Grug Reference-KL Step20 | 0.50 | 43.90 | 44.40 |
| Shared100 | 36.50 | 48.78 | 85.28 |
| Shared075 | 36.00 | 40.65 | 76.65 |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 28.50 | 39.02 | 67.52 |

Parent entries are historical policy references, not freshly repeated matched controls; their NUPA200 scores were extracted from the larger policy panel. Finalist entries are the campaign's completed evaluations. See the [tracker](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md) and [parent subset scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/nupa200/baseline-scores.json). The historical BFCL parent scores are rounded, so these parent sums use the displayed precision. The third finalist recovers less NUPA than the first two. Only Shared100 exceeds the historical BFCL specialist score; Shared075 and Shared050–Attention025 remain below it. These are not matched reruns.

Shared050–Attention025 combines equal NUPA/Base shared-expert weights with 75% NUPA and 25% Base attention-component weights, on top of the selected BFCL expert transfer; it differs from the shared-only 50% variant. [Exact recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared050-attention025-step12.json). Provenance percentages count all stored scalar parameter positions by recipe source: “pure” means copied from that parent, and “blended” means multiple source contributions. They do not measure active parameters or token allocation. In Shared100, the remaining attention, router, embedding, and output-head weights come from NUPA. Blended variants can contain Base contributions even when their pure-Base count is zero.

The metadata ablation swapped the loading/input-preparation file bundle, including tokenizer and chat-template files; it does not isolate individual tokenizer, template, or configuration effects. The 29.00% to 39.00% NUPA200 comparison restored NUPA's native special-token embedding/output rows in a NUPA-weight recipient that previously preserved Base's rows. The [introduction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975)'s response-behavior explanation is a working hypothesis; these experiments do not establish that internal knowledge was unchanged.

Broad capability retention is already in doubt: Shared100 scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus the historical Base references of 95.00% and 67.30%; see the [recorded sentinel scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md). “Sealed” means this merge-search campaign is complete. It does not imply that the full policy evaluation cohort was completed or that follow-up work is ruled out.

🤖

# Implemented merging methods

This catalog covers eleven method families implemented in Marin for the Grug/Snowball 67B campaign; coefficient, density, layer-count, and donor-choice sweeps are configurations within these families. Metadata/tokenizer and special-token-row controls are part of checkpoint construction, not additional merging algorithms. An anchor is the starting checkpoint, donors supply weights or updates, and the recipient is the checkpoint receiving transferred experts; Step92 denotes Snowball Mixed-RLVR, Step12 denotes Grug Antidoom-RLVR1, and Step20 denotes Grug Reference-KL, with exact source revisions preserved in each recipe.

Costs are approximate **arithmetic FLOPs per output checkpoint**, estimated from the implementation with `P = 6.7e10` stored parameters, usually two donors plus an anchor, and approximately `2.0e9` active parameters per token during calibration. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs; comparisons/top-k selection, random-number generation, casts, hashing, storage traffic, and quadratic attention work are excluded, so these are operation-count estimates rather than hardware-profiler measurements.

Wall-clock figures are rounded **observed Iris task durations for representative runs**, including task setup, checkpoint reads, and output writes, but excluding queueing, benchmark evaluation, hyperparameter search, and Hugging Face publication. These timings are not controlled hardware-throughput comparisons: ordinary exports used 16–32 CPU cores; learned calibration and moment collection used eight H100s per job, and their CPU export stages are included explicitly below.

1. **Weighted averaging.** We form a convex combination of aligned parent weights in FP32 and cast the result back to the checkpoint dtype, following the weight-averaging approach of [Model soups (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05482). With two donors and an anchor, our implementation costs approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs (`5P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `avg-050-025-025`.

2. **Task arithmetic and delta amplification.** We subtract an anchor from each donor and add scaled donor updates back to the anchor, including the amplified-update sweeps described by [Task Arithmetic (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04089). The two-donor implementation costs approximately **`5.4e11` FLOPs (`8P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `task-075-075`, with coefficient amplification leaving the arithmetic count unchanged.

3. **TIES merging.** We retain the largest-magnitude updates within each tensor, elect their weighted sign, and average sign-consistent updates using retained coefficient mass, adapting [TIES-Merging (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708) with tensor-local pruning. This costs approximately **`1.3e12` arithmetic FLOPs (`19P`) per merge**, excluding top-k comparisons, and took **85–87 minutes** for the 20% and 80% density configurations.

4. **DARE-linear.** We randomly drop task-vector coordinates, rescale surviving updates by inverse retention probability, and add them to the anchor, following [DARE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099). The dense masked implementation costs approximately **`8.0e11` FLOPs (`12P`) per merge**, excluding random-number generation, and took **48–49 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention.

5. **DARE-TIES.** We apply DARE dropping/rescaling before TIES sign election and sign-consistent aggregation, combining [DARE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099) with [TIES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708). This costs approximately **`1.4e12` FLOPs (`21P`) per merge** and took **49–51 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention, because the implementation still processes dense tensors after masking.

6. **Structured layer and component merging.** We assign tensor-specific coefficients to early/late layers, depth ramps, attention, routed experts, shared experts, routers, normalizations, or output heads, including exact donor replacements through the [campaign checkpoint merger](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/checkpoint.py). Our two-donor code evaluates the dense weighted expression even for zero/one coefficients, costing approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **33 minutes** observed for the `direct-router-step20` representative.

7. **Activation-guided individual-expert transfer.** We favor routed experts used frequently on the target benchmark and infrequently on the other benchmark, then copy or blend their rows while preserving the recipient router, with matched-size random transfers as controls in the [campaign selector](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py). With an existing selection, transferring 16–64 of 256 experts per layer costs approximately **`3.6e11–4.2e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **41–43 minutes** observed for the 16/32-expert exports; the reusable BFCL tool-use replay alone adds approximately **`3.8e16` FLOPs across four separate eight-H100 jobs lasting 4–7 minutes each (about 22 summed job-minutes)**, excluding original benchmark captures and NUPA numeric-response activation collection, so this is not a complete fresh-selection setup cost.

8. **Serial merging.** We materialize an intermediate merge and apply another merge to it, including the top recipe by NUPA200 plus BFCL-Parity percentage-point sum: Step20 routed-expert transfer followed by Step12 shared-expert replacement, as specified in the [winning recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared-step12-100.json). That two-stage construction costs approximately **`7.1e11` FLOPs and 80 minutes per final checkpoint** when both stages are built afresh, or **`3.4e11` FLOPs and 38 minutes** for its second stage when the intermediate already exists, excluding reusable expert selection.

9. **RAM and RAM+.** We classify task-vector coordinates as active when their absolute update exceeds a threshold in one or multiple donors, retain unique updates, average shared updates, and optionally amplify unique contributions using the tensor-local `ramplus_tl` rule from [RAM (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13572) and [mergekit](https://github.com/arcee-ai/mergekit/blob/main/docs/merge_methods.md). Both variants execute approximately **`1.1e12` FLOPs (`16P`) per merge** in our implementation, with **53 minutes** observed for `ram-eps1e4` and **49 minutes** for `ramplus-r010-cap020`.

10. **Behavior-trained coefficients: Expert Merging++ adaptation.** We first learn layer/component coefficients for routed experts, shared experts, attention, and routers, then split flattened weight tensors into importance-allocated contiguous chunks and refine their coefficients to match domain-specific parent hidden states and logits before static export, adapting [Expert Merging / Expert Merging++ (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25712) to native GrugMoE. With 48 calibration examples and 24 warmup plus 96 chunk-training steps, the estimate is approximately **`3.0e14` FLOPs and 7 hours 50 minutes per merge** for `expertpp-hidden`, comprising **7 hours 4 minutes on eight H100s plus 46 minutes of CPU export**, with approximately **`4.0e11` FLOPs** attributable to export alone.

11. **Curvature-aware merging: Optimization Trajectory Aware (OTA) with calibrated tensor-local Fast Fisher Grafting (FFG).** We use square roots of calibrated squared response-loss gradients to weight donor updates and retain coordinates by squared-update-times-moment saliency within each tensor, adapting [OTA + FFG (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11167) because original optimizer moments were unavailable. A fresh two-donor calibration plus the `ota-ffg-d050` export costs approximately **`6.0e13` FLOPs and 3 hours 20 minutes per merge**, comprising **98 minutes of sequential eight-H100 moment collection plus 102 minutes of CPU merging**, while reusing the moments reduces each additional merge to approximately **`1.3e12` FLOPs and 102 minutes**.

The static estimates count the operations actually executed, including coefficient-zero passes; sparsity therefore does not imply proportional FLOP savings. GPU estimates use `2AT` for forward passes and `6AT` for forward/backward passes, where `A` is active parameters per token and `T` is processed tokens, plus full-weight coefficient mixing or moment accumulation: the learned example used 5,233 teacher tokens and 12,936 student tokens, while the two curvature collectors used approximately 4,175 tokens in total.

Evidence: [cost inputs and formulas](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-cost-inputs.json), [recorded Iris durations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-timings/index.json), [arithmetic implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/arithmetic.py), [calibration implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/calibrate.py), and [campaign results](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md).

What we did: Implemented eleven different model merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 checkpoint variants on Snowball 67B A2B with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores.

Why we did it: We observed in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735 that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can have strong and unpredictable effects on non-targeted benchmarks; the reason for this is that it can introduce or repair behavioral pathologies which can radically alter benchmark scores while leaving the underlying model "knowledge" essentially untouched. 

e.g., after RLVR, a model might start outputting every numeric answer such as "31.7" in a corrupted format like "final_answer.31.7" instead of the task's requested "Final Answer: 31.7", resulting in a complete collapse in a benchmark score.

Since we do not want our model to behave pathologically under normal use conditions, we conservatively treat these as model defects to be remedied rather than a benchmark grader defect to be smoothed.  The question, then, is how to remediate such defects most efficiently when each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats at the same time.

Model merging is a popular technique among hobbyists, and there are rumors it is used extensively at frontier labs, but the scientific literature has always been a bit thin. What is unquestionably true is that most model merging methods are extremely FLOP-efficient, in many cases not even requiring GPUs. Since we want to reach the frontier quickly *and* FLOP-efficiently, it would be irresponsible of us not to take a serious look at model merging.

Results: Our target in this case was a Snowball checkpoint which had largely improved but had acquired two severe behavioral defects causing its performance on NUPA and BFCL to degrade dramatically. We used as merge sources two other Snowball models, each of which was an "expert" on one of these benchmarks, but both of which were generally inferior to the student. The merge objective, then, was narrow and challenging; (1) *boost* target model performance on two disparate benchmarks while (2) *avoiding degradation* on non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all of the standard model merging approaches we tried failed at (1) -- the typical pattern was that merging either restored capability weakly on both target benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. After extensive experimentation, we postulated that *sequential merging via selective expert transfer* might retain performance on both benchmarks, and this turned out to be the case, but at a significant cost; we had to discard *essentially all of the parameters from the base model* in the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

Our three most successful merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched source BFCL score, accomplishing (1); but none of these three merges appear to have accomplished (2), and it would be surprising if they did. We will, however, reserve final judgment on this until we have run the complete cohort of policy evals on these checkpoints.

COMMENT: Sequential merging via selective expert transfer is a promising approach for complex MoE merges.

Our most successful strategy used weights from three models to build one model: NUPA, BFCL, folding into Base.

1. We started with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template (more on this later).
2. We then replaced selected routed experts in NUPA with BFCL experts. In each layer, we selected 32 expert positions from BFCL activation measurements and copied the BFCL weights into those positions. *All of the Base routed experts were discarded*.
3. Finally, we changed the NUPA shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We built three separate versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

These percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version produced our highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because the experiments showed that its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model --

- Starting with BFCL: copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts into it gave only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA: copying 32 BFCL-selected experts into it gave 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most of its numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor: the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We did not find a better joint result through those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce.

COMMENT: This was very likely an unusally difficult merge target because our tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

* The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently.

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA’s tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base’s tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers.

This matters for benchmarks, even when the weights are unchanged. The same input text can produce different token IDs. The same output token ID can also decode to different text.

The numerical vocabulary did not change. For example, both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

2. The chat templates formatted tool use differently.

- NUPA’s template presents tool definitions as one JSON array. Base’s template presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA’s template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided. Base’s template omits those IDs.
- The templates also differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Thus, “use the other template” changes the actual input to the model (and therefore benchmarks).

In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input.

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA’s own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

COMMENT: Agent experimental design here was flawed and will require a follow-up study.

The agent drifted from adding specialist capabilities to the Base model almost immediately during the campaign and instead focused on combining the two specialists. We will conduct a follow-up study where we enforce that specialist changes may only target a small, measured fraction of the base model's weights, and perhaps try to control for the tokenizer confound as well.

# Research

The reported 87.04% NUPA200 / 12.19% BFCL-Parity merge uses NUPA as its anchor and discards all Base routed experts; broad policy retention is still unmeasured. With NUPA weights held fixed, changing the configuration and tokenizer moved BFCL-Parity from 0.81% to 17.07%, so model metadata is a material confound. [PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already adds aligned merging and historical artifacts, but its tools do not enforce the later rule that at least 75% of Base weights stay unchanged.

**Relevant code**
- [README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/README.md#L26-L28) — retention and replay limits.
- [select_experts.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py#L19-L56) — ranked and random expert recipes.
- [merge.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/merge.py#L19-L42) — checkpoint merge entry point.

# Proposed Fix

Use #9974 for the follow-up study after review; a second merger implementation would overlap it.

1. Pin the Base, NUPA, and BFCL checkpoint revisions. Keep Base's configuration, tokenizer, chat template, and generation settings fixed for every Base-anchored candidate. Verify tensor and expert-row alignment and specify how donor special-token rows are handled before merging.
2. Audit each export against Base at its stored dtype. Count unchanged scalar weights globally and by component, including embeddings, attention, routers, shared experts, and routed experts; reject candidates that change more than 25% of Base weights.
3. Collect fresh activation measurements, since the archive lacks raw transcripts for exact replay. Compare Base-anchored sequential NUPA/BFCL transfers at predeclared 5%, 10%, and 25% change budgets against matched random expert transfers. Include Base, each specialist, and the prior unconstrained best as reference checkpoints.
4. Evaluate NUPA200, BFCL-Parity, and the complete policy cohort with identical prompts and decoding. Set acceptable non-target regressions before scoring, inspect output-format failures, and publish checkpoint revisions, recipes, changed-weight counts, scores, and negative results. Advance a merge only if it improves both targets within the weight budget and the preregistered retention limits.

## Campaign 2: preserve Base while importing specialist capabilities

TL;DR: We completed 48 additional merges across 12 method families (four variants each), requiring at least 75% of original Base scalar weights and every non-weight model file to remain unchanged. DARE-TIES-02 gave the best observed BFCL + NUPA sum, **45.53**, while changing **6.04%** of Base parameters. Its score was BFCL **45.53%**, NUPA200 **0.00%**; the fresh Base control scored **9.76% / 0.00%** respectively. We improved tool-use performance under the constraint, but did not recover strong performance on both targets together.

[Best checkpoint on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f) · [Implementation PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) · [Reproduction README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/README.md) · [Complete tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/TRACKER.md) · [Unrounded scores, coverage and timings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/results-evidence.json)

NUPA200 tests numerical understanding and arithmetic across number representations, using a fixed 200-item subset of the policy’s 5,000-item set and the pinned loose-format extraction plus exact-match rule. BFCL-Parity uses the 123-trial Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent; its verified solve rate is not the full BFCL leaderboard score.

Base is Grug Antidoom Step12; the NUPA donor is Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92, and the BFCL donor is Grug Reference-KL Step20. The README pins all three revisions. This extends the first campaign's 11 families with ISO-Merger and applies the changed-weight constraint to every family. All 48 construction audits passed; actual changed scalar counts range from **3.02% to 23.50%**. The 25% rule is measured against original Base, including both serial stages; blends count as changed wherever stored bits differ. These constraints do not establish non-target capability retention, which was not evaluated for this cohort.

What worked: DARE-TIES-02 had the highest observed summed target score, with 6.04% of Base parameters changed. DARE-TIES-03 scored 41.46 with 8.34% changed; ISO-03 scored 44.09 with 23.14% changed. DARE-TIES-02 is better on both objectives than either of those alternatives. DARE-linear-02 scored 36.27 with effectively the same changed count as DARE-TIES-02 (14 fewer scalar parameters among about 4.05 billion). Thus the ranking is not just a reward for modifying a larger fraction of Base.

What did not transfer well: learned coefficients, curvature grafting and activation-selected expert transfers did not beat the best DARE-TIES candidate on the summed target metric. Activation-02 had the highest observed NUPA200 score, **10.00%**, but BFCL fell to **5.69%**. The byte-identical serial-02 control scored **7.00% / 5.69%**, showing repeat-run variation. The summed objective also permits a winner with zero NUPA; it does not require balanced capability recovery.

Why remains uncertain. Zero-score trace reviews found both arithmetic errors and correct final numbers accompanied by commentary that failed the fixed response-format rule. Weight changes can affect both capability and response behavior; this study does not isolate their causal contributions. Expert Merging++ and OTA+FFG are native-MoE adaptations trained on 48 independent synthetic calibration examples, and ISO operates on selected expert matrices. Their negative results do not establish that the original methods fail generally. NUPA's exact common ancestor with Base remains unestablished despite aligned tensor coordinates.

All 96 target evaluations are complete under the pinned evaluation policy. These are single-run search results, not statistically resolved method rankings. The campaign is sealed; no further OOD evaluations are planned. The README includes regeneration commands and states the remaining exact-replay gaps: historical calibration tensors and raw evaluation transcripts remain in private storage.

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

comments.body: A precision on the lm_head finding above: those numbers use the H100 d768–d1536 rungs, because the no-lm_head compute table I started from has no d512 entry. With the Oct 3 refit's exact setting (d512–d1536, one floor shared across both mixes and all 15 progress points), removing only the lm_head FLOPs moves the fitted floor from 1.858 to 1.630 (floors within 10% of the minimum SSE span 1.58–1.68) and the forecast from 2.100 to 2.056. So the compute convention accounts for about 0.044 of the 0.061 gap to the Aug 19 pre-registration, about 72%. d512 is where the convention matters most: counting lm_head multiplies its compute by 2.84, against 2.07 at d768 and 1.33 at d1536. Script and output: [addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/2c30e0d892531ae14c1b169e279ca3a8601a0286/addenda/2026-10-09_lm_head_exact_refit.md). The frozen forecast is unchanged.

topics.title: [post-training] Transfer two Snowball experts at once: MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and weight merging
topics.body:
Follow-up to #9920 (single-expert transfer: plain SFT, RS-SFT and OPD each moved the CruxEval expert E's gain back into the Snowball student B). Design note is kept by the owner; this issue is the summary and coordination record.

**TL;DR.** Build a second expert E_2 from B the same way as E, in a different domain (MMLU-Pro), then compare four ways of putting both experts' gains into B at once: multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD from E + E_2), SFT on mixed demos, SFT on rejection-sampled mixed demos, and weight merging of B + E + E_2. Every arm is scored on both domains, so the design also measures forgetting (the domain an arm was not trained for) and collapse (GSM8K, GPQA-D, MATH500). Status: data for E_2 prepared and verified; E_2 training awaits approval; no arm has run.

**Questions.**
1. Do the experts themselves collapse in the other domain after GLM SFT? (E on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D; E_2 on CruxEval; both on GSM8K.)
2. When both experts are transferred into B at once, how much of each domain is recovered and how much of the other is lost?
3. How do MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and merging compare on that, and at what cost?

**Models.** B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5` (unchanged). E = the #9920 CruxEval expert (`…/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`; CruxEval 79.4 / 71.4 vs B 55.4 / 57.8; GPQA-D 44.8% vs B 41.9%, 198 questions × 3 repeats, no observed drop). E_2 = B + full SFT on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe: AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer state, frozen router bias, 32 H100.

**E_2 domain and data.** MMLU-Pro (B 44.1%, GLM 5.3 85.8% under the frozen evaluator). The GLM trace collection had indexed the dataset by question text; 200 questions appear in 2–3 prompt variants, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold letter and 175 GLM grades flipped. Every captured doc was re-joined to the pinned dataset (TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be`) by exact question + ordered options and relabelled; B's stored per-doc labels were independently correct (5,303/12,032 = 44.07% under both label sets). Training subset: a seeded, category-proportional draw of whole question groups (every prompt variant of a picked question travels with it): 1,589 questions = 1,606 docs, 1,359 with a usable GLM trace (correct, finished, reasoning present, fits 32,768 tokens under B's template); 729,901 supervised tokens per epoch. Docs without a usable trace stay in the subset denominator untrained. The other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and scored as a probe. B on the subset 43.9%, on the remainder 44.1%; GLM 85.7% / 85.9%. Artifacts (SHA-pinned, independently verified): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`.

**E_2 gate (operational).** Paired gain over B on the subset ≥ 10 pp as a point estimate and lower 95% group-bootstrap bound ≥ 5 pp on the first pass; if the first pass lands in [8, 10) on the gain or [3, 5) on the bound, one second pass is run and the gate is re-evaluated on both passes pooled (never the better pass). GSM8K paired drop over 2 pp stops the arm. CruxEval, GPQA-D, MATH500 and the held-out score are reported, not gated.

**Frozen evaluator.** As #9920: Evalchemy `c131e5ab`, vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, temperature 1.0 unseeded. MMLU-Pro runs always score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record against the canonical labels, with bootstrap intervals that resample question groups.

**Arms (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the same 3,206 prompts = 1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- MOPD from E + E_2: 4 rollouts per prompt, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (MarinSkyRL routed teachers), one teacher node each.
- Mixed SFT: one demo per prompt (E's sample 0 from the #9920 k=8 CruxEval pool; E_2's sample 0 from a new k=8 collection on the 1,606), the SFT counterpart of MOPD on the same prompts and epochs (prompt-matched, not token-matched).
- Mixed SFT-RS: first execution-correct (CruxEval) or answer-correct (MMLU-Pro) sample per prompt from the two k=8 pools; uncovered prompts stay in the denominators. Uses verifier access the other arms do not have.
- Merge B + E + E_2: #9974 tools with B as anchor and E, E_2 as donors, task arithmetic B + a·(E−B) + b·(E_2−B) over a small coefficient grid plus TIES and DARE-TIES; CPU only, no training.
- Dropped: OPD from E_2 alone and plain SFT from E_2 demos alone (the single-expert question was answered in #9920).

**Selection and reporting.** As #9920: prefer the final checkpoint when it is similar or better on every target metric (similar = paired 95% CI includes 0, an operational threshold); otherwise a second pass on the last two checkpoints and the two-pass means decide. Costs in H100-hours from Iris task durations (method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298); full-run figures labelled as such; demo generation counted once; failed-eval overhead separate. One consolidated final comment; no running log here.

**Budget (planning estimates).** E_2 ≈ 30–40 H100-h; k=8 E_2 demos on 1,606 prompts ≈ 2; MOPD ≈ 300–500 (7 nodes; set by the smoke run); mixed SFT and SFT-RS ≈ 60–120 each; merge CPU only; evaluations ≈ 150.

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-09: MMLU-Pro chosen as E_2's domain (GPQA-D too small to train on: 198 questions). Subset = whole question groups, ~1,600 docs; remainder held out as a probe. GLM labels repaired and verified by two agents; B labels confirmed. Arms fixed to MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merge(B,E,E_2); OPD-from-E_2 and E_2-only SFT dropped. New issue opened rather than continuing in #9920.

🤖
# Research

This is a gated two-domain experiment: the canonical MMLU-Pro data is prepared, but E₂ training awaits approval, and all four transfer arms need the resulting checkpoint. [#9920](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920) supplies the B/E baseline and single-expert recipes; [#9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already implements the checkpoint-merging tools and remains under review. The repository's named evaluation suite does not include working MMLU-Pro or CruxEval tasks, so the frozen Evalchemy configuration from #9920 must be used for comparable scores.

**Relevant code**

topics.title: [iris] Cached job env reaches child jobs after the job scrubs its secrets
topics.body:
Iris caches a job's environment before the job's own code runs, so a job that scrubs secrets from `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` at startup still hands the unscrubbed environment to any non-sandbox child job it launches.

Observed on `cw-us-east-02a` during a Zephyr feasibility spike for Taskforge: the Taskforge queue job removes `GLM_API_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY` and the other host secrets from its environment at start (`scrub_child_environment`), and afterwards both `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` are clean. The job environment Iris had already cached still held `GLM_API_TOKEN` and `WANDB_API_KEY`, so a non-sandbox child job would inherit them. Sandbox children (ShellSim, bwrap, gVisor) received no env in this run; gVisor sandboxes did see the `IRIS_*` variables and the Kubernetes service addresses, including the controller's.

Asks: (1) a documented way for a job to launch children with an explicit environment that does not include the parent's cached env (an allowlist on the child job spec, or a per-submission `inherit_env=False`); (2) sandbox pods should not receive `IRIS_*` variables or the controller's service address unless the submitter asks for them, since model-controlled code runs there.

Related earlier notes on the Taskforge side: CoreWeave `task_env` injecting object-store keys into pods (not reproduced on `cw-rno2a` in this spike) and child jobs inheriting a parent's explicit `-e` secrets.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`build_common_iris_env()` snapshots a job's submitted variables into `IRIS_JOB_ENV`; `get_job_info()` reads that snapshot, and `IrisClient.submit()` merges it into every non-sandbox child. Scrubbing `os.environ` after startup leaves the snapshot intact. #9817 already isolates `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` jobs, including their environment and controller address; the remaining gap is a clean environment for a non-sandbox child.

**Relevant code**
- [`env.py#L291-L295`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/env.py#L291-L295) — serializes submitted variables.
- [`job_info.py#L115-L129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/job_info.py#L115-L129) — loads the cached snapshot.
- [`client.py#L1008-L1014`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/client/client.py#L1008-L1014) — merges parent variables into children.
- [`types.py#L758-L789`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L758-L789) — adds submitter defaults during serialization.

# Proposed Fix

`run task → IRIS_JOB_ENV → get_job_info().env → IrisClient.submit()` is the leak path. Add a per-submission explicit environment mode for non-sandbox children: use only the supplied `EnvironmentSpec.env_vars`, without parent or submitter variables, while preserving setup scripts and placement constraints. Keep inheritance as the default; document the explicit mode and cover the child submission behavior with a regression test. Cluster-wide `task_env` remains governed by the cluster configuration; sandbox isolation is tracked in #9816.

🤖 [PR #9999](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9999) adds an explicit child environment mode and disables Kubernetes service-link injection for SANDBOX pods. The focused environment and pod tests pass (169 cases). The full Iris suite passed 2,873 cases and failed two outside the changed paths; the controller-identity failure also reproduces on `main`.

**Remaining sandbox plan**
1. Split setup/launcher environment from the model-controlled command environment in the Docker worker and Kubernetes task launchers. Remove runtime `IRIS_*` entries before the command starts while preserving any `IRIS_*` variable explicitly supplied by the job.
2. Pass workdir and venv paths needed by the launcher without exporting them to the command, then test the command's observed environment and task setup, status, logs, and exec on both backends.
3. Keep #9997 open until that contract is verified. #9816 tracks the broader sandbox isolation work.

🤖 [PR #9999](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9999) is approved and mergeable, but remains open after the 12-hour review monitor. Its `unit (iris)` failure matches the same test failure on `main`; [the PR comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9999#issuecomment-6088972181) links both CI jobs. The remaining sandbox `IRIS_*` work is planned above, so #9997 remains open.

topics.title: [iris] Take periodic k8s thread dumps without pausing the process
topics.body:
`PeriodicProfiler` dumps every running Kubernetes task pod's threads every 10 minutes. It used py-spy's default `dump`, which stops the target process while it reads the stacks. In a job whose processes synchronize frequently, a pause on any process stalls the others. On a 704-GPU training run, each sweep cost 7–10 s of step time, about 1.3% of throughput.

Periodic dumps now pass `--nonblocking`, so py-spy reads the stacks from the running process. On one GB200 rack (64 training processes), sweeps that dumped one pod at a time cost 0.67–0.93 s of step time with blocking dumps and 0–0.05 s with `--nonblocking`. Scaled to 704 processes, the blocking cost predicts about 9 s per sweep. One of 48 non-blocking pod dumps failed with `Bad address (os error 14)`; the profiler skips a failed capture for that cycle, as it already does for any failed dump. On-demand dumps keep pausing for a consistent read. `build_pyspy_dump_cmd` rejects `--nonblocking` combined with `--native`, which py-spy 0.4.2 refuses.

The change takes effect when the CoreWeave controller restarts; running pods need no restart.
topics.head: 2ecdef1cee302b1e5b673942d0c6fb4ad15c34e5

issue.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens

milestone.title: September: Launch post-trained 67B-A2B to the world

issue.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.
